735: In this independent study course, students pursue advanced research or specialized projects under faculty supervision within their area of interest in computer science. Students develop and execute a structured research plan, applying advanced technical skills and methodologies relevant to their chosen topic, which may span areas such as algorithms, systems, artificial intelligence, or software engineering. Through regular meetings with their faculty advisor, students demonstrate critical thinking, problem-solving abilities, and the capacity to work independently on complex computational challenges. Students produce a comprehensive project report or research paper documenting their findings, methodology, and technical contributions. This course enables students to deepen expertise in specialized domains and prepare for graduate-level work or professional practice in computer science.
807: This course examines the principles and practices of environmental engineering, focusing on water quality management, air pollution control, and waste treatment systems. Students develop proficiency in environmental assessment methodologies, regulatory compliance frameworks, and design of treatment technologies including wastewater systems, air filtration, and solid waste management. The course integrates laboratory work and computational modeling to analyze environmental contaminants and evaluate remediation strategies. Students apply engineering principles to solve real-world environmental problems and design sustainable infrastructure solutions that meet environmental standards and regulations.
814: This course examines the fundamental principles of heat transfer through conduction, convection, and radiation, with emphasis on steady-state and transient thermal analysis. Students develop proficiency in solving heat transfer problems using analytical methods, numerical techniques, and computational tools, including finite difference and finite element analysis. The course covers thermal resistance networks, heat exchangers, and practical applications in mechanical and chemical engineering systems. Students apply theoretical concepts to design and analyze thermal systems, predict temperature distributions, and optimize heat transfer equipment performance. Laboratory work and computational projects reinforce theoretical learning through experimental validation and simulation of real-world thermal processes.
825: This course examines the principles and practices of managing natural, human, and organizational resources within engineering contexts. Students learn quantitative methods for resource allocation, scheduling, and optimization, including techniques such as linear programming, project management frameworks, and cost-benefit analysis. The course covers resource planning tools and software commonly used in engineering projects, with emphasis on sustainability and efficient utilization of materials and labor. Through case studies and practical applications, students develop the ability to identify resource constraints, forecast requirements, and implement strategies that balance technical objectives with economic and environmental considerations. Upon completion, students can apply resource management principles to real-world engineering projects and make data-driven decisions regarding resource allocation.
826: This course examines renewable and alternative energy sources including solar, wind, hydroelectric, geothermal, and biomass technologies as sustainable solutions to global energy demands. Students analyze the thermodynamic principles, conversion efficiency, and environmental impacts of various energy systems while learning to evaluate technical feasibility and economic viability of alternative energy projects. The course covers photovoltaic and solar thermal systems design, wind turbine mechanics, energy storage solutions, and grid integration challenges. Through case studies and design projects, students develop competency in energy modeling software, resource assessment tools, and technical documentation required for alternative energy system implementation. Upon completion, students can assess energy requirements, select appropriate renewable technologies, and design scalable alternative energy solutions for residential, commercial, and industrial applications.
829: Capstone 1 is the first course in a two-semester sequence that requires engineering students to apply theoretical knowledge and practical skills to solve a real-world technical problem. Students work in teams to identify a project scope, conduct literature reviews, perform preliminary design analysis, and develop project plans using industry-standard tools and methodologies. The course emphasizes technical communication, project management, and interdisciplinary collaboration as students present their proposed solutions to faculty advisors and peers. By the end of the course, students will have established a solid foundation for their capstone project, including feasibility studies, resource allocation plans, and initial prototypes or simulations.
916: This course explores advanced techniques for developing high-performance applications across modern computing architectures, including multi-core processors, GPUs, and distributed systems. Students learn parallel programming paradigms such as OpenMP, CUDA, and MPI, along with performance profiling and optimization methodologies to identify and eliminate computational bottlenecks. The course covers memory management strategies, vectorization, and algorithmic optimization to maximize throughput and minimize latency in computationally intensive applications. Through hands-on projects, students implement scalable solutions for real-world problems in scientific computing, data processing, and machine learning, developing proficiency in performance analysis tools and benchmarking frameworks. Upon completion, students are equipped to design, implement, and optimize applications that leverage modern hardware capabilities for demanding computational workloads.
941: This course equips students with practical expertise in acquiring, processing, and analyzing geospatial data using industry-standard tools and methodologies. Students learn remote sensing principles, satellite and aerial imagery interpretation, GPS/GNSS surveying techniques, and LiDAR data collection and processing. The course covers geospatial data quality assessment, validation protocols, and integration of multi-source datasets within GIS environments. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in software platforms such as QGIS, ArcGIS, and specialized remote sensing applications to extract meaningful spatial information for urban planning, infrastructure assessment, and environmental monitoring. Upon completion, students are capable of designing and executing geospatial data acquisition campaigns and producing analysis-ready datasets for decision-making in construction and urban development contexts.
942: This course equips students with advanced skills in creating, designing, and producing digital maps using contemporary GIS software and cartographic principles. Students learn to manipulate geospatial data, apply color theory and visual hierarchy, and implement cartographic generalization techniques to communicate spatial information effectively. The course covers map projection systems, coordinate transformations, and the technical aspects of preparing data for various output formats and platforms. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in tools such as ArcGIS, QGIS, and specialized cartographic software to produce publication-ready maps for professional and academic contexts. Upon completion, students are able to design thematic maps, manage multi-layered spatial datasets, and apply design principles to create visually coherent and analytically sound cartographic products.
943: This course examines the principles and practices of cartographic design within geographic information systems environments. Students learn to create effective maps using GIS software, mastering techniques for data visualization, symbol design, color theory, and map composition. The course covers cartographic representation methods for various data types, including raster and vector data, and explores how to communicate spatial information clearly to diverse audiences. Students develop proficiency in GIS cartography tools and produce publication-ready maps for professional and academic applications. Upon completion, students are able to design, critique, and produce cartographically sound maps that effectively convey spatial analysis results and geographic phenomena.
944: This course provides comprehensive instruction in Global Navigation Satellite Systems (GNSS) technology and its applications within geographic information systems. Students learn the fundamental principles of satellite positioning, signal processing, error sources, and correction techniques including differential GPS and real-time kinematic (RTK) methods. The course covers practical operation of GNSS receivers, field data collection protocols, and post-processing workflows using specialized software. Students develop proficiency in analyzing GNSS datasets, assessing positional accuracy, and integrating satellite-derived coordinates with GIS platforms for spatial analysis and mapping. Upon completion, students are equipped to design and execute GNSS surveys, troubleshoot positioning challenges, and apply satellite positioning data to infrastructure development and spatial planning projects.
945: This course examines the design, implementation, and management of geographic information systems infrastructures at organizational and regional scales. Students learn to architect spatial data repositories, configure server-based GIS platforms, and establish data governance frameworks that support enterprise-level operations. The course covers database design for spatial data, network infrastructure requirements, security protocols, and interoperability standards including OGC web services. Through practical projects, students develop competency in deploying GIS solutions using ArcGIS Server, PostGIS, and open-source alternatives, and in managing spatial data pipelines from acquisition through dissemination. Upon completion, students are prepared to plan and oversee GIS infrastructure projects in government agencies, municipal administrations, and large-scale environmental management organizations.
946: This course provides advanced programming techniques for developing geographic information systems applications and spatial data processing solutions. Students learn object-oriented programming principles using languages such as Python and C++, with emphasis on geospatial libraries, APIs, and frameworks including GDAL, GEOS, and ArcGIS SDK. The curriculum covers spatial algorithms, database connectivity, raster and vector data manipulation, and automation of GIS workflows through scripting. Students develop practical skills in building custom GIS tools, integrating remote sensing data, and creating web-based mapping applications. Upon completion, students are capable of designing and implementing efficient GIS software solutions for complex spatial analysis and data management challenges.
947: This course covers the principles and techniques of digital photography as applied to geospatial data collection and documentation. Students learn camera sensor technology, image acquisition parameters, photogrammetry fundamentals, and the integration of digital imagery into GIS workflows. The course emphasizes practical skills in capturing, processing, and georeferencing aerial and terrestrial photographs for spatial analysis and mapping projects. Students gain proficiency with image processing software, metadata management, and quality control procedures essential for generating reliable geospatial datasets. Upon completion, students are able to acquire, process, and incorporate high-quality digital imagery into GIS projects for urban planning, environmental monitoring, and infrastructure assessment applications.
948: This course examines the integration of Geographic Information Systems with Building Information Modelling technologies to support spatial analysis and infrastructure management. Students learn to work with 3D geospatial data, coordinate systems, and semantic information models that bridge GIS and BIM platforms. The course covers data interoperability standards (IFC, CityGML), spatial databases, and workflows for managing building and urban-scale projects. Students develop practical skills in software tools for GIS-BIM integration, including data conversion, spatial querying, and visualization of multi-scale information. Upon completion, students are able to design integrated systems for urban planning, facility management, and infrastructure assessment that leverage both geospatial and building-level data.
949: This course examines the principles and applications of remote sensing technology and digital image processing techniques for geographic data acquisition and analysis. Students learn to work with multispectral and hyperspectral satellite imagery, applying preprocessing methods such as radiometric correction, geometric registration, and atmospheric correction. The course covers image classification algorithms, change detection methods, and feature extraction techniques using industry-standard software such as ENVI, ERDAS Imagine, and open-source tools like QGIS and Python libraries. Students develop practical skills in interpreting remote sensing data for land use/land cover mapping, environmental monitoring, and urban planning applications. By course completion, students are able to design and execute remote sensing projects that integrate satellite data with GIS workflows for spatial analysis and decision-making.
950: This course provides advanced training in the interpretation and analysis of synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imagery for geospatial applications. Students learn the physical principles of radar remote sensing, including signal processing, polarimetry, and interferometry techniques essential for extracting meaningful information from radar data. The course covers practical decoding methods using industry-standard software tools and algorithms to classify terrain features, detect changes, and generate digital elevation models from radar imagery. Students develop competency in preprocessing raw radar data, applying filtering and enhancement techniques, and validating results against ground truth observations. Upon completion, students are able to independently decode complex radar datasets and integrate SAR-derived information into geographic information systems for land use mapping, disaster monitoring, and infrastructure assessment.
951: This course provides advanced training in statistical methods for analyzing spatially distributed data and predicting values at unsampled locations. Students learn fundamental geostatistical concepts including variography, kriging interpolation techniques (ordinary, universal, and co-kriging), and spatial autocorrelation analysis. The course covers practical applications using industry-standard GIS software and geostatistical packages to model spatial phenomena in environmental monitoring, natural resource assessment, and urban planning. Students develop competency in semivariogram construction, model fitting, and uncertainty quantification for spatial predictions. Upon completion, students can design and execute geostatistical analyses, select appropriate interpolation methods for specific datasets, and communicate spatial uncertainty in professional GIS projects.
952: This course covers the design, development, and deployment of web-based geographic information systems using modern web technologies and GIS frameworks. Students learn to integrate spatial data with web applications using technologies such as JavaScript, mapping libraries (Leaflet, OpenLayers, ArcGIS API), and server-side GIS tools. The course emphasizes client-server architecture, RESTful web services, and real-time data visualization for interactive web maps. Students develop practical skills in publishing geospatial data online, implementing user interfaces for spatial analysis, and optimizing performance for web-based GIS applications. By course completion, students are able to build functional web GIS applications that enable remote access to spatial data and support decision-making across various domains.
953: This course examines the philosophical foundations and methodological frameworks underlying scientific inquiry, with particular emphasis on research design applicable to geographic information systems and spatial analysis. Students engage with epistemological principles, research paradigms, and hypothesis formulation while developing competency in quantitative and qualitative research methodologies relevant to GIS applications. The course covers research planning, data collection protocols, statistical analysis fundamentals, and academic writing standards for spatial science publications. Students will be able to design rigorous research projects, critically evaluate existing GIS studies, and conduct independent research investigations that contribute to the geographic information systems field.
954: This practice course provides students with hands-on experience in applying geographic information systems (GIS) methodologies to real-world spatial problems within architectural and construction contexts. Students work with industry-standard GIS software including ArcGIS, QGIS, and spatial analysis tools to process, analyze, and visualize geospatial data relevant to urban planning, site assessment, and infrastructure development. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in data collection, geodatabase management, cartographic representation, and spatial modeling techniques essential for professional GIS practice. The course emphasizes the integration of GIS analysis with architectural design and construction planning, enabling students to produce actionable spatial intelligence for decision-making in built environment projects. Students complete capstone assignments that demonstrate their ability to conduct independent GIS analyses and communicate findings through professional maps and technical reports.
955: This course equips students with essential project management methodologies and practices tailored to GIS-based initiatives and spatial data projects. Students learn to apply frameworks such as PMBOK, Agile, and Waterfall approaches to plan, execute, monitor, and control GIS projects of varying complexity and scale. The course covers critical areas including scope definition, resource allocation, budget management, risk assessment, stakeholder communication, and quality assurance specific to geospatial technology implementations. Through case studies and practical exercises, students develop competency in using project management tools and software while managing teams working with spatial databases, remote sensing data, and mapping applications. Upon completion, students are prepared to lead GIS projects in government agencies, urban planning organizations, environmental consulting firms, and infrastructure development sectors.
956: This capstone course guides students through the development and defense of an original research thesis under the supervision of a faculty advisor specializing in geographic information systems. Students conduct independent research on advanced GIS topics, applying methodologies such as spatial analysis, remote sensing integration, or geospatial modeling to address real-world problems in urban planning, environmental management, or infrastructure development. The course emphasizes rigorous research design, data collection and processing using GIS software platforms, and critical interpretation of spatial results. Students prepare a comprehensive thesis document and deliver a formal defense presentation to a faculty committee, demonstrating mastery of both technical GIS competencies and scholarly communication. Upon completion, graduates are prepared to contribute original knowledge to the GIS field and pursue professional or academic careers in geospatial science.
957: This course examines fundamental mathematical and computational problems in spherical geometry and their applications in computer science. Students study geometric algorithms for sphere manipulation, including intersection detection, surface parameterization, and spatial partitioning techniques essential for 3D graphics and computational geometry. The course covers both theoretical foundations—such as spherical trigonometry and differential geometry—and practical implementations using computational tools and programming frameworks. Students develop proficiency in solving optimization problems on spherical surfaces and apply these techniques to real-world applications in computer vision, geospatial analysis, and graphics rendering. By course completion, students can model complex spherical problems, implement efficient algorithms for sphere-based computations, and apply these methods to domain-specific challenges in their research or professional work.
958: This course examines the principles and practices of designing, implementing, and managing modern computer networks at enterprise and large-scale levels. Students study network architectures, protocols, routing algorithms, switching technologies, and quality of service mechanisms while gaining hands-on experience with network simulation tools and configuration platforms. The course covers both theoretical foundations in network topology design and practical skills in deploying secure, scalable, and resilient network infrastructure. Students learn to analyze network performance, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and optimize bandwidth allocation using industry-standard tools and methodologies. Upon completion, students are capable of designing comprehensive network solutions that meet organizational requirements for reliability, security, and efficiency.
959: This course examines fundamental principles and practical applications of information security within computing systems and networks. Students study cryptographic algorithms, authentication mechanisms, access control models, and vulnerability assessment techniques while developing hands-on skills in security tools and penetration testing frameworks. The curriculum covers threat modeling, risk analysis, secure coding practices, and compliance standards relevant to modern IT infrastructure. Through laboratory exercises and case studies, students learn to design and implement security architectures, conduct security audits, and respond to cyber incidents. Upon completion, students are equipped to evaluate security risks, develop mitigation strategies, and manage information protection systems in enterprise environments.
960: This course examines the principles and methodologies for designing, analyzing, and maintaining reliable computer systems and software. Students study fault tolerance mechanisms, redundancy strategies, failure detection and recovery techniques, and reliability metrics including Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) and availability calculations. The course covers system modeling approaches such as Markov chains and fault trees, along with practical tools for testing, monitoring, and predicting system behavior under failure conditions. Students apply these concepts to real-world infrastructure scenarios, learning to implement architectural patterns and design decisions that enhance system resilience. Upon completion, students can assess system reliability requirements, design fault-tolerant architectures, and develop strategies to minimize downtime in critical computing environments.
961: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical methodologies of system analysis and operational investigation within complex computational and organizational environments. Students learn to model system behavior, identify performance bottlenecks, and apply quantitative analysis techniques including queuing theory, simulation, and statistical methods to evaluate system efficiency. The course covers system decomposition, requirement specification, data flow analysis, and the use of specialized tools for performance monitoring and optimization. Upon completion, students will be able to conduct comprehensive system audits, design experiments for operational improvement, and develop evidence-based recommendations for system redesign and resource allocation in enterprise and technical infrastructures.
962: This course examines fundamental algorithm design paradigms and their theoretical foundations, including divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms, with emphasis on complexity analysis and correctness proofs. Students study object-oriented software design principles, design patterns, and architectural patterns essential for building scalable systems. The course covers advanced data structures, algorithm optimization techniques, and their implementation in object-oriented languages such as Java or C++. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in applying algorithmic solutions to complex computational problems while adhering to SOLID principles and clean code practices. Upon completion, students can analyze algorithm efficiency, design robust object-oriented systems, and select appropriate algorithmic approaches for real-world software engineering challenges.
963: This course examines the architecture, design, and optimization of high-performance computing (HPC) systems used for computationally intensive applications. Students study parallel processing architectures, including multi-core processors, GPUs, and distributed computing clusters, alongside memory hierarchies, cache optimization, and interconnection networks. The course covers parallel programming models such as OpenMP, MPI, and CUDA, enabling students to develop and optimize applications for HPC environments. Students analyze performance metrics, conduct benchmarking studies, and implement solutions for scientific computing, data analytics, and large-scale simulations. Upon completion, students can design scalable HPC systems, optimize code for parallel execution, and evaluate trade-offs between performance, power consumption, and cost.
964: This course equips students with comprehensive project management methodologies and frameworks essential for leading software development and IT infrastructure initiatives. Students learn industry-standard approaches including Agile, Scrum, Waterfall, and hybrid methodologies, alongside practical tools for scheduling, resource allocation, risk management, and stakeholder communication. The course covers project planning, scope definition, budget estimation, quality assurance protocols, and team coordination techniques specific to technology projects. Students develop competency in using project management software platforms and gain hands-on experience through case studies and real-world project simulations. Upon completion, students are prepared to manage complex IT projects from inception through delivery, making informed decisions about methodology selection and resource optimization in professional environments.
965: This course covers the architecture, design principles, and programming of microcontroller systems used in embedded applications. Students study microcontroller hardware components including processors, memory systems, input/output interfaces, and peripheral devices, alongside the software development lifecycle for embedded systems. The course emphasizes practical programming in assembly language and C, focusing on interrupt handling, timer management, analog-to-digital conversion, and real-time system constraints. Students develop proficiency with microcontroller development tools, debuggers, and simulation environments while implementing control algorithms for industrial and consumer applications. By course completion, students design and program functional embedded systems that interface with sensors and actuators in real-world scenarios.
966: This course examines the philosophical foundations of scientific inquiry and the systematic methodologies underlying research in computer science and informatics. Students engage with epistemological principles, research paradigms, and the structure of scientific knowledge while developing competency in research design, hypothesis formulation, and experimental validation. The course covers quantitative and qualitative research methods, statistical analysis, and data interpretation techniques applicable to computational problems. Students learn to critically evaluate existing literature, construct rigorous research proposals, and communicate findings through academic publications and presentations. Upon completion, students are equipped to conduct independent research projects, contribute to peer-reviewed scholarship, and apply evidence-based methodologies to complex informatics problems.
967: This course examines the principles and practices of designing, testing, and maintaining reliable software systems. Students study fault tolerance mechanisms, failure analysis, software testing methodologies including unit testing, integration testing, and system testing, as well as quality assurance frameworks and metrics. The course covers reliability modeling, defect prediction techniques, and debugging strategies using industry-standard tools and version control systems. Students apply these concepts through practical projects involving test automation, continuous integration pipelines, and reliability assessment of real-world applications. Upon completion, students will be able to design robust software architectures, implement comprehensive testing strategies, and evaluate software reliability using quantitative metrics.
968: This course equips students with advanced mathematical modeling techniques for solving complex engineering problems using computational methods. Students learn to formulate engineering challenges as mathematical models, apply numerical analysis methods, and implement solutions using industry-standard software packages such as MATLAB, ANSYS, and COMSOL. The curriculum covers finite element analysis, differential equations solving, optimization algorithms, and data visualization for engineering applications. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in translating real-world engineering scenarios into computational simulations and interpreting results for design and decision-making. Upon completion, students can independently model, simulate, and analyze engineering systems across multiple domains including structural mechanics, fluid dynamics, and thermal analysis.
969: This course examines the architecture, design, and implementation of large-scale data processing systems used in modern computing environments. Students study distributed computing frameworks such as Hadoop and Spark, learning how to process petabyte-scale datasets across clustered computing resources. The course covers key concepts including data partitioning, fault tolerance, MapReduce programming models, and SQL-on-Hadoop technologies like Hive and Presto. Students develop practical skills in data pipeline construction, performance optimization, and working with NoSQL databases designed for big data applications. Upon completion, students can design and deploy scalable data systems, implement efficient data processing workflows, and analyze performance characteristics of distributed computing solutions.
970: This course examines contemporary software tools and frameworks essential for developing artificial intelligence applications. Students gain practical experience with machine learning libraries (TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn), natural language processing toolkits, and computer vision frameworks while implementing algorithms for classification, regression, clustering, and deep learning tasks. The course covers version control systems, containerization technologies, and cloud-based AI platforms for scalable model deployment and management. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in data preprocessing, model training, hyperparameter optimization, and performance evaluation. Upon completion, students can architect and deploy production-ready AI solutions using industry-standard tools and best practices.
971: This practice course provides students with hands-on experience applying informatics and computer science concepts in professional environments. Students engage in real-world software development projects, systems design, and computational problem-solving under the guidance of industry practitioners and faculty supervisors. The course develops practical competencies in programming languages, software engineering methodologies, database management, and collaborative development tools relevant to contemporary IT industry standards. Students complete substantial projects that demonstrate their ability to design, implement, and deploy technical solutions while documenting their work and presenting results to stakeholders. This capstone experience bridges academic theory with professional practice, preparing graduates for careers in software development, systems architecture, and technology innovation.
972: This course examines the principles and applications of computer-aided design (CAD) and building information modeling (BIM) systems used in architectural and construction projects. Students learn to operate industry-standard software tools such as AutoCAD, Revit, and specialized parametric design platforms while developing proficiency in 2D drafting, 3D modeling, and data management workflows. The course covers automation techniques, template creation, scripting, and integration of design systems with project management and construction documentation processes. Students apply these skills to develop complete design documentation sets, optimize design workflows through automation, and collaborate effectively in digital project environments. Upon completion, students are capable of managing complex architectural projects using integrated digital design systems and implementing automation strategies to enhance productivity in professional practice.
973: This course examines the intersection of software engineering principles and market dynamics, equipping students with methodologies to develop commercially viable software products. Students learn to apply engineering rigor to market analysis, competitive positioning, and product-market fit validation while integrating technical architecture decisions with business strategy. The course covers demand forecasting, technology adoption curves, pricing models, and go-to-market strategies specific to software systems. Through case studies and project work, students develop skills in translating market requirements into technical specifications and managing the trade-offs between feature complexity, time-to-market, and resource constraints. Upon completion, students can lead cross-functional teams in delivering software products that satisfy both technical excellence and market viability criteria.
974: Students engage in independent research and thesis development under the guidance of a faculty supervisor, culminating in a comprehensive written thesis and public defense. The course emphasizes advanced problem-solving in computer science, requiring students to conduct original research, apply rigorous methodologies, and contribute novel insights to their chosen specialization within informatics. Students develop proficiency in research design, literature review, technical documentation, and academic presentation while working on substantial computational or theoretical projects. Through iterative feedback sessions and formal defense preparation, students refine their ability to communicate complex technical findings to both specialist and general audiences. Upon completion, students demonstrate mastery of their research domain and readiness for professional or doctoral-level work in computer science.
975: This course develops students' proficiency in modern Armenian language and cultivates effective communication skills within professional and academic contexts. Students study the structure and evolution of Armenian, including phonetics, grammar, and vocabulary, while examining Armenian cultural heritage and its influence on contemporary discourse. The course emphasizes practical writing and oral presentation techniques essential for technical documentation, academic papers, and professional communication in the IT field. Through analysis of authentic texts and guided practice, students learn to construct clear, precise arguments and adapt their communication style to diverse audiences. Upon completion, students will demonstrate advanced competency in Armenian language use and the ability to communicate complex technical concepts effectively in their native language.
976: This course examines the political, social, cultural, and economic development of Armenia from ancient times through the modern era. Students explore key historical periods including the Hellenistic and Roman eras, the establishment of Christianity as the state religion, the medieval kingdom, Ottoman and Russian imperial rule, and the formation of the modern Armenian state. The course emphasizes Armenia's contributions to architecture, literature, and technology, with particular attention to how historical events have shaped contemporary Armenian society and identity. Through primary source analysis and historical documentation, students develop critical thinking skills applicable to understanding how historical context influences technological and infrastructural development in their field.
977: This course develops proficiency in Russian language communication for computer science students in an academic and professional context. Students study Russian grammar, vocabulary, and syntax while engaging with technical texts, documentation, and specialized terminology relevant to computing and information technology fields. Through reading, writing, listening, and speaking activities, students build competency in understanding Russian-language academic materials, technical manuals, and professional communications. The course emphasizes practical application of language skills for international collaboration, accessing Russian scientific literature, and professional development in the global technology sector.
978: This course covers fundamental mathematical concepts essential for computer science applications, including differential and integral calculus, linear algebra, and analytical geometry. Students develop proficiency in solving systems of linear equations, computing derivatives and integrals, and applying vector and matrix operations to computational problems. Through problem-solving exercises and practical applications, students gain the mathematical foundations necessary for advanced coursework in algorithms, graphics programming, and numerical methods. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and computational techniques, enabling students to model and analyze complex systems encountered in software development and computer engineering.
979: This course covers fundamental principles of mechanics, thermodynamics, electricity, magnetism, and waves essential for computer science applications. Students engage with classical and modern physics concepts through theoretical analysis and laboratory experiments, developing problem-solving skills in kinematics, energy conservation, electromagnetic fields, and oscillatory systems. The course emphasizes mathematical modeling and computational approaches to physical phenomena, enabling students to understand the physical constraints and principles underlying hardware design and computational systems. Through practical demonstrations and calculations, students gain proficiency in applying physics principles to real-world engineering problems relevant to information technology infrastructure and digital systems.
980: This course provides foundational knowledge in computer science principles and their practical applications within the built environment context. Students learn core programming concepts, algorithms, data structures, and computational thinking through hands-on coding projects using languages such as Python and C++. The course covers essential topics including problem-solving methodologies, software development fundamentals, and basic database design relevant to architectural and construction informatics systems. Students develop proficiency in writing efficient code, debugging programs, and applying computational logic to real-world scenarios in architecture and construction technology. By course completion, students are able to design and implement software solutions, analyze algorithmic complexity, and apply programming skills to domain-specific informatics challenges.
981: This course examines fundamental principles of civil defence and emergency management systems relevant to infrastructure and construction sectors. Students study hazard identification, risk assessment methodologies, and emergency response protocols for natural disasters, industrial accidents, and other critical incidents affecting built environments. The course covers evacuation procedures, shelter design standards, communication systems during emergencies, and coordination mechanisms between civil protection agencies and construction organizations. Students develop competencies in emergency planning, crisis management decision-making, and implementation of safety measures in construction projects and urban infrastructure. Upon completion, students are prepared to integrate civil defence considerations into construction projects and contribute to organizational emergency preparedness strategies.
982: This course provides students with the fundamental principles of orthographic projection and spatial visualization essential for architectural and engineering design. Students learn to represent three-dimensional objects through multiple projection planes, including plan, elevation, and section views, while developing proficiency in constructing geometric relationships such as intersections, tangencies, and transformations. The course covers classical descriptive geometry methods including point, line, and plane operations in space, as well as practical applications in technical drawing and CAD-based representation. Through both manual drafting and digital tools, students acquire the ability to interpret complex spatial problems and communicate design intent through standardized technical drawings. This foundational knowledge enables students to transition effectively into advanced courses in computer graphics, architectural design, and engineering visualization.
983: This course introduces students to core economic principles and their applications in the context of technology and business. Students examine microeconomic concepts including supply and demand, market structures, consumer behavior, and firm decision-making, alongside macroeconomic topics such as national income, inflation, unemployment, and monetary policy. The course develops competency in economic analysis tools, including graphical analysis, basic statistical methods, and quantitative modeling of economic phenomena. Students apply economic reasoning to evaluate technology sector dynamics, cost-benefit analysis for IT projects, and resource allocation decisions relevant to computing professionals. Upon completion, students can analyze economic trade-offs in software development, infrastructure investment, and digital business models using fundamental economic frameworks.
984: This course provides students with a comprehensive overview of computer science fundamentals and career pathways within the discipline. Students explore core areas including algorithms, data structures, programming paradigms, and computational theory while gaining exposure to emerging specializations such as artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, and software engineering. The course introduces essential development tools and environments, including version control systems and integrated development platforms, enabling students to establish foundational technical competencies. Through practical projects and case studies, students develop problem-solving skills and learn to apply computational thinking to real-world challenges. By course completion, students can articulate their specialization interests, understand professional opportunities in the field, and demonstrate basic proficiency in fundamental programming and algorithmic concepts.
985: This course develops students' physical fitness and motor skills through structured exercise and athletic training. Students engage in cardiovascular conditioning, strength training, flexibility work, and sport-specific techniques to build overall health and endurance. The course emphasizes proper exercise form, injury prevention, and personal fitness assessment. Upon completion, students demonstrate improved physical conditioning and the ability to design and maintain personalized fitness routines that support sustained academic and professional performance.
986: This course examines the structure, history, and contemporary usage of the Armenian language within its cultural and social contexts. Students develop proficiency in formal and informal communication registers, technical terminology in computer science, and professional writing conventions essential for academic and workplace settings. The course explores Armenian linguistic traditions, cultural communication norms, and the role of language in preserving national identity. Through practical exercises, students strengthen their oral presentation skills, written composition abilities, and cross-cultural communication competencies. Upon completion, students are able to communicate effectively in Armenian across diverse professional and academic contexts while understanding the cultural dimensions of language use.
987: This course examines the political, social, cultural, and economic development of Armenia from ancient times through the modern era. Students analyze key historical periods including the Hellenistic and Roman epochs, the establishment of Christianity as the state religion, the medieval kingdom period, and Armenia's experience under Ottoman and Russian rule. The course emphasizes Armenia's contributions to architecture, literature, and science, with particular attention to how historical events have shaped Armenian identity and contemporary society. Through primary source analysis and historical documentation, students develop critical thinking skills applicable to understanding how cultural and historical contexts influence technological and societal development. This foundational knowledge supports informed citizenship and provides essential context for understanding Armenia's role in regional and global affairs.
988: This course develops students' proficiency in a foreign language, typically English, with emphasis on technical and academic communication relevant to computer science and information technology fields. Students acquire vocabulary and grammatical structures necessary for reading technical documentation, understanding programming-related literature, and engaging with international academic discourse. The course combines language skills development with domain-specific content, enabling students to comprehend and produce written and oral communication in professional computing contexts. Upon completion, students will be able to read technical manuals, participate in international academic discussions, and communicate effectively in professional IT environments.
989: This course covers fundamental mathematical concepts essential for computer science applications, including linear algebra, calculus, and discrete mathematics. Students develop proficiency in matrix operations, eigenvalue problems, differential and integral calculus, and mathematical logic necessary for algorithm analysis and computational theory. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving techniques and mathematical modeling of real-world computational systems. 1167: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of formal logic and its applications in computer science.
