The course covers fundamental concepts including satisfiability, validity, and completeness, with emphasis on their relevance to automated reasoning and knowledge representation. Through practical exercises, students learn to formalize natural language statements into logical expressions and apply logical reasoning to solve computational problems. Upon completion, students are able to construct formal proofs, analyze logical arguments, and apply logical principles to algorithm design and program verification.
1168: This course extends the foundational concepts of single-variable calculus to multivariable functions and infinite series. Students study partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and convergence of series, applying these tools to optimize multivariable functions and solve real-world problems in physics and engineering. The course develops proficiency in computing line and surface integrals, understanding gradient and divergence operators, and analyzing the behavior of power series and Taylor expansions. Through problem-solving and computational practice, students gain the mathematical foundation necessary for advanced courses in differential equations, physics, and machine learning algorithms used in computer science applications.
1169: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of probability theory and their applications in computer science. Students learn discrete and continuous probability distributions, conditional probability, Bayes' theorem, and random variables, with emphasis on computational applications. The course covers key concepts including expectation, variance, and the law of large numbers, alongside practical techniques for statistical inference and hypothesis testing. Through problem-solving and programming exercises, students develop the ability to model uncertainty, analyze algorithms probabilistically, and apply stochastic methods to real-world computational problems. This foundation prepares students for advanced coursework in machine learning, data science, and algorithm analysis.
1170: This course introduces students to the fundamental mathematical tools and techniques essential for computer science applications. Students study set theory, logic, graph theory, combinatorics, and number theory, with emphasis on their computational relevance and algorithmic implications. The course develops proficiency in formal proof techniques, including mathematical induction and proof by contradiction, while exploring practical applications in algorithm design and complexity analysis. Through problem-solving exercises and computational implementations, students learn to model discrete structures and apply mathematical reasoning to solve real-world computing problems. By course completion, students can formalize computational problems mathematically and select appropriate discrete mathematical tools for algorithm development and analysis.
1171: This course provides an intensive exploration of Python programming fundamentals and advanced techniques for computer science applications. Students master core concepts including data structures, object-oriented programming, functional programming paradigms, and algorithm design while developing proficiency with industry-standard tools and libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib. Through hands-on projects and problem-solving exercises, students learn to write efficient, maintainable code and apply computational thinking to real-world challenges. Upon completion, students are capable of developing robust Python applications, implementing complex algorithms, and leveraging Python's ecosystem for data analysis and scientific computing.
1172: This course introduces students to low-code and no-code development platforms that enable rapid application development with minimal hand-coding. Students explore leading platforms such as Microsoft Power Apps, Salesforce Lightning, and Mendix, learning to design data models, create user interfaces through visual builders, and implement business logic using declarative programming approaches. The course covers application architecture patterns, integration with existing systems via APIs, and deployment strategies for enterprise environments. By the end of the course, students can develop functional business applications, automate workflows, and deliver solutions quickly while understanding the trade-offs between low-code platforms and traditional software development.
1173: This course introduces students to enterprise systems architecture and organizational knowledge management within modern business environments. Students learn to analyze enterprise resource planning (ERP) systems, business process modeling, and information systems governance while developing practical skills in system design and implementation. The course covers key frameworks for enterprise architecture, data management strategies, and knowledge documentation practices essential for IT professionals. Through case studies and project work, students apply theoretical concepts to real-world enterprise challenges, gaining hands-on experience with enterprise software platforms and business intelligence tools. Upon completion, students are equipped to design scalable information systems, optimize business processes, and contribute effectively to enterprise digital transformation initiatives.
1174: This course equips students with practical statistical methods essential for data analysis and decision-making in computer science applications. Students learn probability theory, descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and statistical inference using both parametric and non-parametric approaches. The course emphasizes hands-on implementation using statistical software packages such as R or Python, enabling students to analyze real-world datasets and interpret results critically. Students develop competency in designing experiments, validating statistical assumptions, and communicating findings through visualizations and reports. By course completion, students can apply appropriate statistical techniques to solve computational problems and support evidence-based conclusions in software development and data-driven projects.
1175: This course covers fundamental mathematical structures essential for computer science, including set theory, logic, graph theory, and combinatorics. Students develop proficiency in formal proof techniques, Boolean algebra, and algorithmic analysis through rigorous problem-solving. The course emphasizes applications to computer science such as complexity analysis, network modeling, and discrete optimization. Students learn to construct and verify mathematical arguments, analyze algorithmic correctness, and apply discrete structures to real-world computational problems. Upon completion, students are equipped to tackle advanced courses in algorithms, data structures, and theoretical computer science.
1176: This course introduces students to fundamental programming concepts through the C language, emphasizing low-level memory management, pointers, and efficient code design. Students learn syntax, control structures, functions, arrays, and dynamic memory allocation while developing problem-solving skills applicable to systems programming and embedded systems. The course covers essential debugging techniques, compilation processes, and best practices for writing maintainable code. Through practical assignments and projects, students gain proficiency in implementing algorithms, manipulating data structures, and optimizing performance-critical applications. Upon completion, students are able to write, test, and debug standalone C programs and understand how high-level programming concepts translate to machine-level operations.
1177: This foundational course introduces students to the core principles and practices of computer science within a comprehensive digital sciences framework. Students explore fundamental concepts including algorithms, data structures, computational logic, and programming paradigms while developing proficiency in multiple programming languages and development environments. The course covers essential topics such as software engineering principles, database design, and system architecture, enabling students to design and implement scalable solutions to computational problems. Through hands-on projects and practical assignments, students gain experience in problem-solving methodologies, code optimization, and collaborative development practices. Upon completion, students are prepared to advance to specialized courses in software development, artificial intelligence, networks, and other computer science domains.
1178: This course covers fundamental principles of classical and modern physics essential for computer science applications. Students explore mechanics, thermodynamics, electromagnetism, and quantum mechanics, with emphasis on physical phenomena underlying computational systems and digital technologies. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students develop analytical skills in applying mathematical models to physical systems and understanding the hardware constraints of computing devices. The course provides the theoretical foundation necessary for advanced studies in computer architecture, signal processing, and computational physics.
1179: This course introduces students to fundamental management principles and organizational practices essential for technology professionals and IT project leaders. Students examine organizational structures, strategic planning, resource allocation, and decision-making frameworks within the context of software development and technology companies. The course covers project management methodologies, team dynamics, budget management, and performance metrics specific to IT environments. Through case studies and practical exercises, students develop skills in planning, coordinating technical teams, and managing software development projects. Upon completion, students will be able to apply management concepts to real-world scenarios in technology organizations and lead technical teams effectively.
1180: This course introduces students to digital manufacturing technologies and their practical applications in product design and production. Students learn computer-aided design (CAD) software, 3D modeling, and simulation tools essential for manufacturing workflows. The course covers additive manufacturing (3D printing), subtractive processes, and digital fabrication techniques, with hands-on experience using CNC machines and 3D printers. Through project-based learning, students design, prototype, and manufacture physical components, developing skills in translating digital designs into tangible products. By course completion, students can independently conceptualize products, create technical models, and execute manufacturing processes using industry-standard digital tools.
1181: This course introduces students to fundamental numerical techniques for solving mathematical problems that lack analytical solutions. Students learn to implement algorithms for root-finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and solving systems of linear and nonlinear equations using programming languages such as Python or C++. The course covers error analysis, convergence criteria, and stability considerations essential for reliable computational results. Through practical assignments, students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate numerical methods for specific problems and analyzing their computational efficiency and accuracy. Upon completion, students are able to apply numerical methods to real-world engineering and scientific problems and implement robust numerical solutions in software applications.
1182: This course introduces students to formal logic and its foundational principles essential for computer science. Students learn propositional logic, truth tables, logical equivalences, and methods of proof including direct proof, proof by contradiction, and mathematical induction. The course covers predicate logic, quantifiers, and formal reasoning systems that underpin algorithm design and program verification. Through practical exercises, students develop the ability to construct rigorous logical arguments, translate natural language into formal notation, and apply logical reasoning to solve computational problems. By course completion, students can analyze logical structures, evaluate the validity of arguments, and apply formal logic techniques to computer science applications such as database queries and constraint satisfaction problems.
1183: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of information theory and its applications in computer science. Students study key concepts including entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, and source coding, with emphasis on Shannon's fundamental theorems. The course covers practical applications such as data compression algorithms, error-correcting codes, and cryptographic principles. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students develop the ability to quantify information content, analyze communication system efficiency, and design coding schemes for reliable data transmission. Upon completion, students can apply information-theoretic principles to optimize data storage, transmission, and security in real-world computing systems.
1184: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of digital information processing and computer architecture. Students learn how data is represented in binary systems, how logic gates and Boolean algebra form the basis of digital circuits, and how these components combine to create functional computing units. The course covers combinational and sequential logic design, memory hierarchies, and the basic fetch-execute cycle of processors. Through hands-on exercises and simulations, students develop proficiency in designing simple digital circuits and understanding how high-level programs translate into machine-level operations. By the end of the course, students can analyze digital systems at the gate level, design basic circuits using hardware description languages or schematic tools, and explain how information flows through a computer system from input to output.
1185: This course covers fundamental algorithmic concepts and design paradigms essential to computer science. Students study algorithm analysis using Big O notation, complexity classes, and performance optimization techniques. The curriculum includes sorting and searching algorithms, graph algorithms, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches, with emphasis on correctness proofs and runtime analysis. Through practical implementation in languages such as Python or C++, students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate algorithms for specific computational problems and analyzing their efficiency trade-offs. Upon completion, students can design, implement, and evaluate algorithms for real-world applications while understanding their computational complexity and limitations.
1186: This course introduces students to object-oriented programming using C# and the .NET framework. Students learn core programming concepts including classes, inheritance, polymorphism, and exception handling while developing practical applications. The course covers essential tools such as Visual Studio, LINQ for data queries, and asynchronous programming patterns. Students gain proficiency in building console applications, Windows Forms applications, and working with databases through ADO.NET. By course completion, students can design and implement robust C# applications following industry best practices and object-oriented design principles.
1187: This capstone project course requires students to design and implement a substantial software system that integrates concepts from core computer science disciplines. Working individually or in small teams, students apply software engineering principles including requirements analysis, system architecture, design patterns, and version control to develop a complete application. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving, code quality, documentation, and presentation skills through iterative development cycles and peer review. Students deliver a functional prototype with accompanying technical documentation and demonstrate their project through formal presentation and demonstration sessions.
1188: Systems 1 introduces students to the fundamental principles of computer systems architecture and operating system concepts. Students learn about processor organization, memory hierarchies, instruction sets, and the basics of process management, file systems, and inter-process communication. Through hands-on programming assignments in C and assembly language, students develop practical skills in low-level system programming and gain insight into how operating systems manage hardware resources. By the end of the course, students can analyze system performance, write efficient code that interacts directly with hardware, and understand the trade-offs between abstraction and efficiency in system design.
1189: This course builds on foundational architecture concepts to explore advanced processor design, memory hierarchies, and system-level optimization techniques. Students examine instruction-level parallelism, pipelining, cache coherence protocols, and virtual memory management through both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. The course covers modern CPU architectures, including superscalar and multi-core designs, alongside performance analysis methodologies and hardware description languages for circuit simulation. Students develop the ability to analyze architectural trade-offs, predict system performance, and design efficient computing systems that balance speed, power consumption, and cost constraints.
1190: Logic 2 builds on foundational logical reasoning to explore advanced topics in formal logic, including predicate logic, modal logic, and proof systems. Students learn to construct and evaluate complex logical arguments using symbolic notation, truth tables, and natural deduction techniques. The course covers applications of logic in computer science, such as automated theorem proving, logic programming, and formal verification of algorithms. Through practical exercises and problem sets, students develop proficiency in translating natural language statements into formal logical expressions and determining logical validity and consistency. By course completion, students can apply sophisticated logical reasoning to analyze computational problems and understand the theoretical foundations underlying programming languages and artificial intelligence systems.
1191: This course provides students with essential algebraic foundations and mathematical modeling techniques for computer science applications. Students study linear algebra, abstract algebra, Boolean algebra, and discrete mathematical structures, with emphasis on their computational relevance and algorithmic applications. The course covers matrix operations, vector spaces, group theory, and formal logic, equipping students to model and solve computational problems mathematically. Through practical exercises and programming implementations, students develop proficiency in translating real-world problems into algebraic frameworks and applying symbolic computation tools. Upon completion, students are able to construct mathematical models for algorithmic design, analyze computational complexity using algebraic methods, and apply formal mathematical reasoning to software development and data structure design.
1192: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and architecture of computer networks. Students study the OSI model, TCP/IP protocol suite, and network layers, gaining hands-on experience with packet analysis tools such as Wireshark and network simulation software. The course covers essential topics including IP addressing, subnetting, routing protocols, and switching mechanisms, with practical exercises in configuring network devices and analyzing network traffic. By the end of the course, students are able to design basic network topologies, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and understand how data is transmitted across modern communication networks.
1193: This course examines the principles and practices of designing effective human-computer interfaces and interactive systems. Students explore user-centered design methodologies, usability evaluation techniques, and cognitive psychology foundations that inform interface design decisions. The course covers prototyping tools, wireframing, user research methods, and accessibility standards (WCAG, ARIA) to ensure inclusive design. Through hands-on projects, students apply iterative design processes, conduct usability testing, and analyze user feedback to refine interactive applications. Upon completion, students can evaluate existing interfaces critically, design user-centered solutions for real-world problems, and justify design choices based on human factors principles.
1194: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of algorithm design, analysis, and implementation across multiple programming paradigms. Students learn to evaluate algorithmic efficiency using Big O notation, master control structures and data organization techniques, and develop proficiency in at least two programming languages such as Python and C++. The course covers fundamental algorithms including sorting, searching, and graph traversal, alongside core programming concepts including functions, recursion, object-oriented principles, and memory management. Through practical programming assignments and problem-solving exercises, students develop the ability to translate algorithmic concepts into efficient, maintainable code and analyze trade-offs between different computational approaches.
1195: This capstone project course requires students to design and implement a substantial software application that integrates concepts from core computer science coursework. Students work individually or in small teams to develop a complete system, applying software engineering principles including requirements analysis, system design, testing, and documentation. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving, code quality, version control systems, and project management methodologies. Upon completion, students deliver a functional application with comprehensive technical documentation and demonstrate their ability to independently manage the full software development lifecycle.
1196: Systems 2 builds on foundational operating systems concepts to explore advanced process management, memory hierarchies, and inter-process communication mechanisms. Students examine kernel architecture, scheduling algorithms, virtual memory implementation, and synchronization primitives through both theoretical analysis and hands-on system programming in C. The course covers file systems, I/O subsystems, and network stack fundamentals, with emphasis on understanding performance trade-offs and resource allocation strategies. Students develop multi-threaded applications, debug system-level issues, and optimize code for modern multi-core processors. By course completion, students can design efficient system software, diagnose performance bottlenecks, and implement concurrent solutions to real-world computing problems.
1197: This course examines advanced topics in computer architecture, building on foundational knowledge of processor design and organization. Students study instruction-level parallelism, cache hierarchies, memory management systems, and performance optimization techniques used in modern processors. The course covers pipeline design, branch prediction, out-of-order execution, and virtual memory implementation through both theoretical analysis and practical simulation tools. Students analyze real processor architectures and learn to evaluate trade-offs between performance, power consumption, and cost. By the end of the course, students can design and optimize processor components, predict system performance, and understand the architectural decisions in contemporary computing systems.
1198: This course examines the theoretical foundations of computational complexity and algorithmic efficiency. Students study complexity classes including P, NP, and NP-completeness, learning to classify problems by their computational difficulty and prove hardness results. The course covers fundamental techniques such as reduction methods, approximation algorithms, and parameterized complexity to analyze and solve computationally challenging problems. Through problem sets and proofs, students develop the ability to determine whether problems are tractable, identify appropriate algorithmic approaches, and understand the limits of efficient computation. This knowledge is essential for designing practical solutions in software engineering and recognizing when problems require specialized techniques beyond standard algorithms.
1199: This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and design principles of relational databases. Students learn data modeling techniques, including entity-relationship (ER) diagrams, and normalization theory to design efficient database schemas. The course covers Structured Query Language (SQL) for data definition, manipulation, and querying, with practical exercises using industry-standard database management systems such as PostgreSQL or MySQL. Students develop the ability to create normalized database designs, write complex SQL queries, and understand transaction management and basic indexing strategies. By the end of the course, students can design relational databases from requirements specifications and implement them using SQL.
1200: This course builds on foundational networking concepts to explore advanced topics in network architecture, protocols, and design. Students study the OSI model's upper layers, focusing on transport and application layer protocols including TCP/IP, DNS, HTTP, and SMTP, while examining network security fundamentals such as encryption, authentication, and firewalls. Through hands-on laboratory work using packet analysis tools like Wireshark and network simulation software, students configure routers and switches, troubleshoot connectivity issues, and implement basic network services. The course develops practical skills in network administration, performance optimization, and vulnerability assessment, preparing students to design and maintain secure, scalable network infrastructures.
1201: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practices of object-oriented programming (OOP) using industry-standard languages such as Java or C++. Students learn core concepts including classes, objects, inheritance, polymorphism, encapsulation, and abstraction through hands-on coding assignments and projects. The course covers essential design patterns, memory management, and debugging techniques while emphasizing clean code practices and software design principles. By the end of the course, students are able to design and implement well-structured programs using OOP methodologies, refactor procedural code into object-oriented solutions, and apply inheritance hierarchies to solve complex programming problems. This foundational course prepares students for advanced software development and serves as a prerequisite for subsequent programming courses in the Computer Science curriculum.
1202: This course introduces students to fundamental data structures essential for efficient algorithm design and software development. Students learn to implement and analyze arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, understanding their performance characteristics through Big O notation. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving through hands-on programming assignments in languages such as C++ or Python, where students construct data structures from scratch and apply them to real-world computational problems. By course completion, students can select appropriate data structures for specific applications, optimize code performance, and solve complex algorithmic challenges using structured data organization techniques.
1203: Project S4 is a capstone course where students apply core computer science concepts to design and implement a substantial software system. Students work in teams to develop applications using modern programming languages, version control systems, and software engineering methodologies learned throughout the program. The course emphasizes requirements analysis, system architecture, testing strategies, and documentation practices essential for professional development. Students deliver a fully functional project with accompanying technical documentation and present their work to faculty and peers, demonstrating competency in collaborative problem-solving and technical communication.
1204: This course introduces students to low-level programming concepts and operating system fundamentals through hands-on systems development. Students learn memory management, process control, inter-process communication, and file I/O operations using C and assembly language. The course covers system calls, kernel interfaces, and the design of efficient algorithms for resource-constrained environments. Through practical projects, students develop system utilities, implement concurrent programs, and optimize code for performance and reliability. Upon completion, students are able to write robust systems software, debug complex memory issues, and understand how applications interact with operating system kernels.
1205: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of parallel computing on multi-core and distributed systems. Students learn fundamental concepts including thread management, synchronization mechanisms, race conditions, and deadlock prevention using languages such as C++ and Python with OpenMP and MPI libraries. The course covers shared-memory parallelization techniques, message-passing architectures, and performance optimization strategies including load balancing and communication minimization. Through practical assignments, students develop concurrent applications, analyze parallel efficiency metrics, and debug multi-threaded programs on modern hardware. Upon completion, students are able to design scalable parallel algorithms, implement thread-safe code, and evaluate performance trade-offs in parallel systems.
1206: This course introduces students to functional programming paradigms and their application to abstract data type design. Students learn core functional concepts including immutability, first-class functions, higher-order functions, and recursion, typically using languages such as Haskell or Lisp. The course covers fundamental abstract data types including lists, trees, stacks, and queues, emphasizing their functional implementations and algebraic specifications. Through practical exercises, students develop the ability to design efficient algorithms using pattern matching, lazy evaluation, and functional composition while analyzing their computational complexity. By course completion, students can write correct, maintainable functional code and apply abstract data type principles to solve complex programming problems.
1207: This course introduces students to probability theory and statistical methods essential for data analysis in computer science applications. Students learn fundamental concepts including probability distributions, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis, with emphasis on practical implementation using statistical software packages such as R and Python. The course covers exploratory data analysis techniques, descriptive statistics, and inferential statistics methods for drawing conclusions from datasets. Through hands-on projects and case studies, students develop proficiency in data visualization, statistical modeling, and interpreting results in real-world contexts. Upon completion, students are able to design statistical analyses, select appropriate methods for different data types, and communicate findings effectively using computational tools.
1208: This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and algorithms of graph theory, covering topics such as graph representations, connectivity, paths, cycles, and tree structures. Students learn to analyze graph properties using adjacency matrices and adjacency lists, and implement classical algorithms including depth-first search, breadth-first search, Dijkstra's shortest path, and minimum spanning tree algorithms. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical applications, enabling students to model real-world problems as graphs and solve them computationally. Through programming assignments and problem-solving exercises, students develop proficiency in designing efficient graph-based solutions and analyzing their time and space complexity. By course completion, students can apply graph theory to optimize networks, analyze social structures, and solve combinatorial problems in computer science applications.
1209: This course examines the theoretical foundations of computation through the study of automata and formal languages. Students explore finite automata, pushdown automata, and Turing machines, understanding their computational capabilities and limitations. The course covers regular languages, context-free languages, and recursively enumerable languages, along with their corresponding grammar formalisms and recognition mechanisms. Students develop proficiency in constructing automata, proving language properties, and analyzing the decidability and complexity of computational problems. Upon completion, students can model computational processes formally, design automata for language recognition, and apply automata theory to compiler design and language processing applications.
1210: This course covers advanced networking concepts and protocols essential for designing and managing complex network infrastructures. Students study routing algorithms, network security mechanisms, quality of service (QoS) implementation, and wireless networking technologies, building on foundational networking knowledge. Through hands-on laboratory work, students configure routers and switches, analyze network traffic using packet analysis tools such as Wireshark, and implement network security policies. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving in network troubleshooting, performance optimization, and protocol implementation. Upon completion, students can design scalable network architectures, diagnose network issues, and apply security best practices in enterprise environments.
1211: This course builds upon foundational OOP concepts to develop advanced programming skills using object-oriented design principles and patterns. Students explore inheritance hierarchies, polymorphism, abstract classes, and interfaces while implementing complex software architectures in languages such as Java or C++. The course covers design patterns (creational, structural, and behavioral), SOLID principles, and refactoring techniques to write maintainable, scalable code. Through practical projects, students apply these concepts to develop multi-class applications, manage dependencies, and optimize object interactions. Upon completion, students can design robust object-oriented systems, implement enterprise-level software solutions, and critically evaluate code quality using industry-standard practices.
1212: This capstone project course requires students to design and implement a substantial software system that integrates concepts from previous coursework in algorithms, databases, and software engineering. Students work in teams to manage the full development lifecycle, including requirements analysis, system architecture design, implementation, testing, and documentation. The course emphasizes practical application of design patterns, version control systems, and collaborative development practices using industry-standard tools. Upon completion, students deliver a fully functional application with comprehensive technical documentation and demonstrate their ability to solve complex computational problems through systematic software engineering methodologies.
1213: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical applications of computer graphics, image processing, and analysis techniques. Students learn core concepts including color models, image filtering, edge detection, feature extraction, and image segmentation using both spatial and frequency domain methods. The course combines theoretical foundations with hands-on programming using industry-standard tools such as OpenGL for graphics rendering and libraries like OpenCV or MATLAB for image processing. Students develop practical skills in implementing algorithms for image enhancement, transformation, and analysis while understanding the mathematical foundations of linear algebra and signal processing that underpin these techniques. By course completion, students can design and implement graphics applications, process digital images for various applications, and analyze visual data using computational methods.
1214: This course explores functional programming paradigms and their application to designing abstract data types (ADTs) in languages such as Haskell or Lisp. Students learn core concepts including immutability, higher-order functions, pattern matching, and recursive data structures, while mastering techniques for composing functions and reasoning about program correctness through type systems. The course covers implementation of fundamental ADTs—lists, trees, graphs, and custom algebraic data types—using functional approaches, emphasizing lazy evaluation and memory efficiency. Through practical assignments, students develop the ability to write modular, testable code that leverages type safety and functional composition to solve complex computational problems. By course completion, students can design and implement sophisticated data structures using functional principles and apply these techniques to real-world software engineering challenges.
1215: This course introduces students to the fundamental theory and practical applications of signal processing in digital systems. Students learn to analyze continuous and discrete-time signals using Fourier analysis, filtering techniques, and spectral methods, with emphasis on real-world signal manipulation and noise reduction. The course covers the design and implementation of digital filters, sampling theory, and the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) algorithm using industry-standard tools such as MATLAB or Python. Through laboratory work and projects, students develop the ability to process audio, image, and sensor data, and to apply signal processing techniques to solve engineering problems in telecommunications, audio processing, and biomedical applications.
1216: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of professional software development, covering the complete software development lifecycle from requirements analysis to deployment and maintenance. Students learn industry-standard methodologies including Agile, Scrum, and waterfall approaches, alongside design patterns, version control systems (Git), and collaborative development workflows. The course emphasizes practical skills in code organization, testing strategies (unit testing, integration testing), and documentation standards essential for team-based projects. Through hands-on projects, students develop the ability to design scalable architectures, implement quality assurance processes, and communicate technical decisions effectively with both technical and non-technical stakeholders.
1217: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of cybersecurity principles, threats, and defense mechanisms essential for protecting information systems. Students learn cryptographic techniques, authentication protocols, network security, and secure coding practices while analyzing real-world attack vectors including malware, social engineering, and exploitation methods. The course covers security architecture design, vulnerability assessment, and penetration testing methodologies using industry-standard tools and frameworks. Through hands-on labs and case studies, students develop practical skills in implementing firewalls, intrusion detection systems, and access control mechanisms. Upon completion, students are equipped to identify security risks, design secure systems, and respond to cybersecurity incidents in professional environments.
1218: This course builds on foundational database concepts to explore advanced relational database design, implementation, and optimization techniques. Students study normalization theory, transaction management, concurrency control, and query optimization while working with industry-standard database management systems such as PostgreSQL and MySQL. The course covers SQL programming at an advanced level, including stored procedures, triggers, and views, alongside practical experience with database administration tasks and performance tuning. Students design and implement complex multi-table databases, analyze query execution plans, and apply indexing strategies to improve system efficiency. By course completion, students can architect scalable database solutions, troubleshoot performance issues, and manage real-world database systems in production environments.
1219: This course introduces students to the foundational concepts and practical applications of artificial intelligence within computer science. Students explore machine learning algorithms, neural networks, natural language processing, and computer vision, gaining hands-on experience with Python libraries such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, and scikit-learn. The curriculum covers supervised and unsupervised learning techniques, model evaluation, and optimization methods essential for building intelligent systems. By course completion, students can design and implement AI solutions for real-world problems, evaluate model performance, and apply deep learning architectures to complex datasets.
1220: This internship course provides students with practical professional experience in computer science through placement in industry, research institutions, or technology companies. Students apply theoretical knowledge from their coursework to real-world projects, developing technical competencies in software development, systems design, or other specialized areas relevant to their placement. The course emphasizes professional communication, project management, and collaborative problem-solving within organizational contexts. Students complete a formal internship report documenting their contributions, technical achievements, and professional development. Upon completion, students demonstrate readiness for entry-level positions in software engineering, systems administration, or related computer science fields.
1221: This course examines the principles and practices of parallel computing architectures and programming models essential for modern AI applications. Students learn to design and implement parallel algorithms using frameworks such as OpenMP, MPI, and CUDA, while studying shared-memory and distributed-memory computing paradigms. The course covers performance analysis, scalability optimization, and synchronization techniques for multi-core and GPU-accelerated systems. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in parallelizing computationally intensive machine learning workloads and neural network training pipelines. Upon completion, students can architect efficient parallel solutions for large-scale data processing and deep learning applications.
1222: This course equips students with computational methods and mathematical foundations essential for machine learning applications. Students learn numerical algorithms, linear algebra optimization techniques, and statistical inference methods while implementing solutions in Python and specialized libraries such as NumPy, SciPy, and scikit-learn. The course covers matrix computations, gradient descent variants, and probabilistic modeling approaches that underpin modern machine learning systems. Through practical projects, students develop proficiency in data preprocessing, algorithm implementation, and performance evaluation on real-world datasets. Upon completion, students can design and optimize machine learning pipelines, select appropriate algorithms for specific problems, and apply scientific computing techniques to solve complex AI challenges.
1223: This course covers advanced algorithmic techniques essential for solving complex computational problems in artificial intelligence and machine learning contexts. Students study graph algorithms, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and approximation algorithms, with emphasis on analyzing time and space complexity using asymptotic notation. The course includes practical implementation of algorithms in Python or C++, with applications to real-world AI problems such as optimization, pathfinding, and resource allocation. Students develop proficiency in algorithm design paradigms and learn to select appropriate algorithmic approaches for specific problem classes. By course completion, students can analyze algorithmic efficiency, implement sophisticated algorithms, and apply algorithmic thinking to AI-related challenges.
1224: This course examines the mathematical foundations of formal language theory and its applications to computational linguistics and compiler design. Students study regular languages, context-free grammars, and Turing machines, developing proficiency in automata theory and formal language classification. The course covers lexical analysis, parsing techniques, and the theoretical limits of computation, with practical implementation of lexers and parsers using tools such as Flex and Bison. Students apply these concepts to natural language processing tasks and gain insight into the decidability and complexity properties essential for designing programming languages and AI systems that process human or machine-generated text.
1225: This course equips students with practical methodologies for designing and implementing AI systems in collaborative environments. Students learn software engineering principles tailored to machine learning projects, including requirements analysis, architecture design, and version control systems (Git). The course covers modeling techniques such as UML for AI systems, design patterns for scalable applications, and best practices for code organization and documentation. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in collaborative development workflows, code review processes, and continuous integration/deployment pipelines. Upon completion, students are able to architect robust AI solutions, manage complex codebases in team settings, and implement professional development practices essential for production-grade machine learning systems.
1226: This course introduces students to the fundamental techniques and tools for processing multimodal data including images, audio, and text. Students learn core concepts in digital signal processing, image filtering and transformation, audio feature extraction, and natural language processing fundamentals, utilizing libraries such as OpenCV, librosa, and NLTK. The course covers practical applications including image segmentation, speech analysis, and text tokenization through hands-on programming assignments in Python. By the end of the course, students are able to preprocess and extract meaningful features from diverse data types, prepare datasets for machine learning pipelines, and implement basic data processing workflows essential for AI applications.
1227: This foundational course introduces students to core artificial intelligence concepts and methodologies essential for advanced study in AI systems. Students explore classical AI approaches including search algorithms, knowledge representation, logical reasoning, and constraint satisfaction problems, alongside practical implementations using Python and relevant AI libraries. The course covers both theoretical foundations and hands-on applications, enabling students to develop intelligent agents and solve real-world problems using symbolic AI techniques. By course completion, students will be able to design and implement AI solutions for complex problems, evaluate different algorithmic approaches, and understand the limitations and capabilities of classical AI methods. This course provides the essential groundwork for subsequent specialized AI courses in the program.
1228: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and techniques of computer graphics, covering geometric transformations, rasterization, and rendering pipelines. Students learn to implement graphics algorithms using modern APIs such as OpenGL or WebGL, working with vertex and fragment shaders to control the visualization process. The course covers essential topics including coordinate systems, projection matrices, lighting models, and texture mapping. Through practical programming assignments, students develop the ability to build interactive 3D applications and understand the mathematical foundations underlying real-time graphics systems. By course completion, students can create visually complex scenes and optimize rendering performance for computational efficiency.
1229: This course examines the design, implementation, and analysis of systems composed of multiple autonomous agents that interact and coordinate to achieve individual or collective goals. Students explore fundamental concepts including agent architectures, communication protocols, negotiation mechanisms, and distributed decision-making algorithms. The course covers practical applications such as robotic swarms, game-theoretic modeling, and collaborative problem-solving environments, with hands-on projects using multi-agent simulation frameworks and platforms. Students develop competency in implementing agent-based models, analyzing emergent behaviors, and applying game theory and mechanism design to real-world scenarios. By course completion, students can architect scalable multi-agent systems and evaluate their performance in complex, dynamic environments.
1230: This capstone course requires students to conduct original research in artificial intelligence under faculty supervision, culminating in a substantial written thesis and presentation. Students apply advanced machine learning, deep learning, and AI methodologies to address real-world problems or theoretical questions within their chosen specialization. The course develops critical competencies in research design, experimental validation, literature synthesis, and academic communication through iterative feedback and peer review. Students gain hands-on experience with contemporary AI frameworks, datasets, and computational resources while learning to evaluate the limitations and ethical implications of their work. Upon completion, students produce a research contribution suitable for publication or industry application, demonstrating mastery of both technical depth and scholarly rigor in artificial intelligence.

Students gain hands-on expertise in tools and frameworks commonly used in AI development, such as deep learning libraries, data processing pipelines, and cloud computing platforms. Through this experience, students develop professional competencies in project management, technical communication, and collaborative problem-solving within the context of artificial intelligence applications. The internship culminates in a comprehensive report and presentation demonstrating the student's ability to bridge theoretical knowledge with practical implementation in AI-focused environments.
1232: This capstone course requires students to conduct original research or develop an advanced artificial intelligence application under faculty supervision. The course culminates in a comprehensive written thesis and oral presentation that demonstrates mastery of AI methodologies and domain-specific knowledge acquired throughout the program. Students gain practical experience in project management, technical documentation, and communicating complex AI concepts to both specialist and non-specialist audiences.
1233: This course examines the fundamental principles of computer architecture and their application to graphics processing systems. Students study CPU design, memory hierarchies, instruction sets, and parallel processing architectures while learning how graphics processing units (GPUs) optimize rendering pipelines and parallel computation. The course covers raster and vector graphics algorithms, 3D transformations, lighting models, and shader programming using modern graphics APIs such as OpenGL or DirectX. Through practical projects, students implement graphics applications that leverage hardware acceleration and develop proficiency in graphics libraries and optimization techniques for real-time rendering. Upon completion, students can design efficient graphics systems, understand hardware-software interactions in visual computing, and apply architectural principles to optimize graphics performance.
1234: This course covers the fundamental principles of mechanics applied to engineering problems and computational modeling. Students study kinematics, dynamics, statics, and energy methods, with emphasis on solving real-world problems using both analytical and numerical approaches. The course integrates computational tools such as MATLAB and finite element analysis software to simulate mechanical systems and validate theoretical predictions. Students develop proficiency in formulating differential equations of motion, analyzing forces and stresses in structures, and optimizing mechanical designs. Upon completion, students can model complex mechanical systems, apply conservation principles to engineering applications, and implement computational solutions for mechanics-based problems in software development and systems design.
1235: This course introduces students to fundamental principles of electrical engineering essential for computer science professionals. Students study circuit analysis, electromagnetic theory, and basic semiconductor physics, learning to analyze DC and AC circuits using Kirchhoff's laws, Thevenin's theorem, and phasor methods. The course covers power systems, transformers, and electric machines at an introductory level, providing context for how electrical systems support computing infrastructure. Through laboratory work, students develop practical skills in circuit measurement, breadboarding, and simulation using tools such as SPICE or equivalent software. Upon completion, students understand electrical fundamentals necessary for hardware design, embedded systems development, and informed collaboration with electrical engineers in technology projects.
1236: Mathematical Analysis 3 covers advanced topics in multivariable calculus and real analysis, including partial derivatives, multiple integrals, and vector calculus. Students develop proficiency in computing directional derivatives, gradient vectors, and Jacobian matrices for functions of several variables, with applications to optimization problems. The course emphasizes rigorous proofs of convergence theorems, continuity properties, and the inverse and implicit function theorems in multidimensional spaces. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students master techniques for evaluating double and triple integrals using various coordinate systems and applying Green's theorem, Stokes' theorem, and the divergence theorem. Upon completion, students are equipped to analyze complex mathematical models used in computer graphics, machine learning, and scientific computing.
1237: This course introduces students to MATLAB as a fundamental computational tool for scientific and engineering applications. Students learn core programming concepts including variables, data types, control structures, functions, and vectorized operations within the MATLAB environment. The course covers matrix operations, basic data visualization through plotting functions, and file input/output operations essential for data processing. Through hands-on exercises and projects, students develop proficiency in writing efficient MATLAB scripts and functions to solve mathematical and computational problems. By course completion, students are able to implement algorithms, manipulate numerical data, and create visualizations for scientific computing tasks.
1238: This course covers the theory and applications of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) and partial differential equations (PDEs) essential for computer science applications. Students study first-order and higher-order differential equations, linear systems, stability analysis, and numerical methods for solving differential equations computationally. The course emphasizes practical problem-solving using analytical techniques and computational tools, with applications to modeling dynamic systems, algorithms, and computational simulations. Students develop proficiency in both symbolic and numerical approaches, learning to implement solutions using programming languages and mathematical software. Upon completion, students can formulate differential equation models for real-world problems, select appropriate solution methods, and implement efficient numerical algorithms for computational applications.
1239: This course covers the theory and applications of complex-valued functions, including complex numbers, analytic functions, and the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Students study contour integration, residue theory, and conformal mappings, developing the mathematical foundations essential for advanced computational and signal processing applications. The course emphasizes both theoretical proofs and practical problem-solving techniques, enabling students to apply complex analysis to engineering problems in electromagnetics, fluid dynamics, and control systems. Through rigorous exercises and applications, students master techniques for evaluating difficult integrals and solving differential equations using residue calculus. Upon completion, students are equipped to apply complex analysis methods in algorithm development, numerical computation, and theoretical computer science.
1240: This course sequence covers fundamental probability theory and mathematical statistics essential for computer science applications. Students learn probability axioms, discrete and continuous distributions, random variables, expectation, variance, and limit theorems including the Central Limit Theorem. The course develops practical skills in statistical inference, hypothesis testing, confidence intervals, and regression analysis using both theoretical derivations and computational methods. Students apply these concepts to real-world datasets and learn to implement statistical algorithms in programming environments commonly used in data analysis and machine learning. Upon completion, students can model stochastic processes, analyze experimental data rigorously, and make informed decisions based on statistical evidence in software engineering and algorithmic contexts.
1241: This course examines the mathematical foundations and solution techniques for partial differential equations (PDEs) that govern physical phenomena. Students study classical PDEs including the wave equation, heat equation, and Laplace equation, along with analytical methods such as separation of variables, Fourier series, and Laplace transforms. The course develops competency in applying boundary value problems, eigenvalue problems, and integral transform methods to model and solve real-world physical systems. Students gain practical experience implementing numerical solutions using computational tools and analyzing the mathematical properties of solutions including existence, uniqueness, and stability. Upon completion, students can formulate physical problems as mathematical equations and select appropriate analytical or computational methods for their solution.
1242: This course covers the fundamental theory of functional analysis, focusing on infinite-dimensional vector spaces and linear operators. Students study Banach spaces, Hilbert spaces, and their properties, including completeness, compactness, and orthogonality. The course develops rigorous mathematical foundations for spectral theory, eigenvalue problems, and applications to differential and integral equations. Through theoretical proofs and computational exercises, students learn to analyze convergence properties, apply fixed-point theorems, and solve operator equations essential for advanced numerical methods and quantum mechanics applications in computer science.
1243: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of mathematical logic and formal reasoning systems. Students study propositional logic, predicate logic, logical inference rules, and proof techniques including natural deduction and resolution methods. The course covers truth tables, logical equivalences, quantifiers, and the relationship between syntax and semantics in formal systems. Through practical problem-solving, students develop the ability to construct rigorous mathematical proofs, analyze logical arguments for validity, and apply formal logic to computer science applications such as program verification and knowledge representation. By course completion, students can formalize problems using logical notation and evaluate the correctness of logical systems.
1244: This course examines fundamental algorithmic concepts and computational problem-solving techniques essential to computer science. Students study algorithm design paradigms including divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy algorithms, alongside formal analysis methods for evaluating time and space complexity using Big-O notation. The course covers sorting and searching algorithms, graph algorithms, and NP-completeness theory, providing theoretical foundations for understanding computational limits and problem tractability. Through problem sets and implementation exercises, students develop the ability to analyze algorithm efficiency, select appropriate algorithmic approaches for specific problems, and prove correctness of algorithmic solutions. Upon completion, students can design efficient algorithms, recognize intractable problems, and apply theoretical knowledge to optimize real-world computational systems.
1245: Discrete Mathematics 1 and 2 provide foundational knowledge in mathematical structures essential for computer science. Students study set theory, logic, relations, functions, graph theory, combinatorics, and number theory, developing rigorous proof techniques including mathematical induction and direct/indirect proofs. The course emphasizes algorithmic thinking and the mathematical foundations underlying data structures, algorithms, and computational complexity analysis. Through problem-solving exercises, students learn to model computational problems mathematically and analyze their properties. Upon completion, students can apply discrete mathematical concepts to design efficient algorithms, prove program correctness, and solve complex computational problems.
1246: Mathematical Programming 1,2 covers the theory and applications of optimization techniques for solving complex computational problems. Students learn linear programming formulations, the simplex method, duality theory, and sensitivity analysis, along with integer programming and branch-and-bound algorithms. The course introduces students to modeling real-world optimization problems in resource allocation, production planning, and network design, and provides hands-on experience with optimization software tools and solvers. Upon completion, students can formulate optimization problems mathematically, select appropriate solution methods, and implement algorithms to find optimal solutions for practical engineering and business applications.
1247: Students in Digital Methods 1 and 2 develop foundational competencies in computational problem-solving and algorithmic thinking through structured programming and data structure design. The course covers fundamental programming paradigms, control flow, functions, arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, and basic sorting and searching algorithms, utilizing languages such as C++ or Python. Students implement solutions to computational problems, analyze algorithm efficiency using Big O notation, and apply debugging techniques to validate code correctness. By course completion, students can design and implement efficient algorithms, select appropriate data structures for specific applications, and write well-documented, maintainable code suitable for real-world software development projects.
1248: This course covers the fundamental concepts and applications of differential geometry with emphasis on computational methods and practical problem-solving. Students study curves and surfaces in Euclidean space, learning to compute curvature, torsion, and geodesics using calculus and linear algebra techniques. The course introduces manifolds, differential forms, and tensor calculus as tools for modeling geometric structures in physics and engineering applications. Students develop proficiency in mathematical software for visualizing geometric objects and performing symbolic computations. Upon completion, students can analyze geometric properties of complex surfaces, apply differential geometric methods to optimization problems, and utilize these concepts in computer graphics, robotics, and computational physics.
1249: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical applications of error-correcting codes in digital communication and data storage systems. Students study linear codes, Hamming codes, cyclic codes, and convolutional codes, learning to analyze code performance through metrics such as minimum distance, code rate, and Shannon capacity. The course covers encoding and decoding algorithms, including syndrome decoding and Viterbi decoding, with emphasis on real-world implementations in telecommunications and storage media. Students develop proficiency in designing codes for specific channel conditions and evaluating trade-offs between error correction capability, computational complexity, and bandwidth efficiency. Through theoretical analysis and computational projects, students gain the ability to select and implement appropriate coding schemes for practical communication systems.
1250: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical applications of information theory, including entropy, mutual information, and channel capacity. Students study data compression techniques, error-correcting codes, and cryptographic principles essential for secure communication systems. The course covers Shannon's theorems and their implications for designing efficient communication protocols and storage systems. Through problem sets and programming assignments, students develop skills in analyzing information-theoretic bounds, implementing compression algorithms, and evaluating system performance. Upon completion, students can apply information-theoretic concepts to optimize data transmission, assess system reliability, and design secure information systems in real-world applications.
1251: This course covers advanced programming concepts and techniques essential for professional software development. Students learn object-oriented programming principles, design patterns, and algorithmic problem-solving using languages such as C++ or Java. The course emphasizes data structure implementation, memory management, and code optimization through hands-on projects and coding assignments. Upon completion, students can design and implement complex software systems, apply design patterns to real-world problems, and write efficient, maintainable code following industry standards.
1252: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical techniques of web application development using modern programming languages and frameworks. Students learn front-end technologies including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, alongside back-end development with server-side languages such as PHP, Python, or Node.js, and database design with SQL. The course emphasizes responsive design, RESTful API development, security best practices, and version control systems like Git. Through hands-on projects, students develop full-stack web applications, implement user authentication and authorization mechanisms, and deploy applications to production environments. Upon completion, students are able to design, develop, test, and maintain dynamic web applications that meet industry standards.
1253: This course examines the fundamental principles and design of Electronic Computing Machines (EHMs), covering processor architecture, memory hierarchies, and instruction set design. Students study digital logic components, CPU organization, control units, and data path implementation through both theoretical analysis and practical design exercises. The course emphasizes how hardware components interact to execute machine instructions and how architectural decisions impact computational performance. Through hands-on projects, students design and simulate simple processor architectures, gaining proficiency with hardware description languages and computer architecture simulation tools. Upon completion, students understand how software instructions map to hardware execution and can analyze trade-offs in processor design decisions.
1254: This course covers fundamental and advanced programming paradigms, languages, and development methodologies essential for modern software engineering. Students learn multiple programming languages (such as C++, Python, and Java), object-oriented design principles, functional programming concepts, and software development best practices including version control systems and debugging techniques. The course emphasizes practical application through hands-on projects, teaching students to design, implement, and optimize algorithms while understanding performance trade-offs and code maintainability. By course completion, students can develop robust applications across different domains, select appropriate technologies for specific problems, and collaborate effectively using industry-standard development tools and workflows.
1255: This course covers the design and implementation of low-level software systems that interact directly with computer hardware and operating system kernels. Students learn assembly language programming, memory management, process and thread control, inter-process communication, and file system operations using C and x86/ARM assembly. The course emphasizes understanding system calls, kernel interfaces, and performance optimization through hands-on development of utilities, device drivers, and system-level applications. Upon completion, students can write efficient system software, debug complex hardware-software interactions, and design scalable concurrent programs for modern computing architectures.
1256: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of operating system design principles, architecture, and implementation. Students study process management, memory management, file systems, input/output operations, and concurrency control mechanisms including synchronization and deadlock prevention. Through hands-on programming assignments in C/C++, students implement core OS components such as process schedulers, memory allocators, and file system operations on both Linux and custom kernel environments. The course covers both theoretical concepts and practical system-level programming, enabling students to understand how operating systems manage hardware resources and provide abstractions for application software. Upon completion, students can analyze OS performance, debug system-level issues, and design efficient solutions for resource allocation and process coordination.
1257: This course covers fundamental and advanced concepts in computational geometry, focusing on geometric algorithms and their applications in computer science. Students learn to design and implement algorithms for solving geometric problems such as convex hulls, polygon triangulation, point location, and spatial searching using data structures like quadtrees and k-d trees. The course emphasizes mathematical foundations including coordinate geometry, vector operations, and computational complexity analysis while developing practical programming skills in C++ or Python. Students apply these techniques to real-world problems in computer graphics, geographic information systems, and computational physics. By course completion, students can analyze geometric problems, select appropriate algorithmic approaches, and implement efficient solutions for spatial data processing.
1258: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of database design, implementation, and management principles. Students learn relational database theory, normalization techniques, and SQL for querying and manipulating data across multiple tables. The course covers database architecture, indexing strategies, transaction management, and concurrency control to ensure data integrity and system performance. Through hands-on projects using industry-standard database management systems such as PostgreSQL or MySQL, students develop practical skills in schema design, query optimization, and database administration. Upon completion, students are able to design normalized databases, write efficient SQL queries, implement data security measures, and troubleshoot common database performance issues.
1259: This course provides students with a comprehensive foundation in designing and analyzing fundamental data structures and algorithms essential for software development. Students learn to implement and evaluate core data structures including arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, understanding their performance characteristics and appropriate use cases. The course covers algorithm design paradigms such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches, with emphasis on time and space complexity analysis using Big O notation. Through practical programming assignments, students develop proficiency in selecting optimal data structures and algorithms for specific computational problems and gain hands-on experience with algorithm implementation and testing. Upon completion, students are able to analyze algorithmic efficiency, design scalable solutions to complex problems, and apply appropriate data structures in real-world software engineering contexts.
1260: This course introduces students to the practical development and implementation of software applications across diverse domains. Students learn to design, code, and deploy applications using contemporary programming languages and development frameworks relevant to industry standards. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in version control systems, testing procedures, and collaborative development practices. Upon completion, students are equipped to build functional applications, troubleshoot technical issues, and contribute effectively to professional software development teams.

The course covers algorithm design paradigms such as divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, and greedy approaches, along with complexity analysis using Big-O notation. Students implement algorithms in a programming language to solve computational problems, develop proofs of correctness, and analyze time and space efficiency. Through hands-on projects, students develop the ability to design normalized databases, write complex SQL queries, optimize database performance, and implement secure data management solutions for real-world applications. 1265: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of engineering modeling within information technology contexts. The course covers model formulation, simulation techniques, validation methods, and performance analysis across mechanical, electrical, and software systems. By course completion, students are able to construct accurate predictive models, conduct system simulations, and make data-driven engineering decisions for real-world IT applications.
1266: This course examines the social, ethical, and legal dimensions of information technology development and deployment in contemporary society. Through case studies and collaborative discussions, students learn to communicate ethical concerns to technical and non-technical audiences and advocate for responsible IT practices. Upon completion, students will be equipped to integrate ethical reasoning into their professional IT careers and contribute to socially conscious technology innovation.
1267: This course examines the principles and practices of managing and regulating network infrastructure within organizational and regulatory frameworks. Students study network administration protocols, quality of service (QoS) management, bandwidth allocation, and compliance with international standards and telecommunications regulations. The course covers practical tools for network monitoring, configuration management, and performance optimization using industry-standard platforms. Students develop competency in implementing network policies, managing security protocols, and ensuring regulatory compliance in enterprise environments. Upon completion, students can design and maintain managed network systems that meet organizational requirements and regulatory standards.
1268: This course examines the principles and practices of IT resource planning within organizational contexts. Students learn to assess IT infrastructure needs, forecast resource requirements, and optimize allocation of hardware, software, and personnel across enterprise systems. The course covers capacity planning methodologies, cost-benefit analysis, budgeting frameworks, and tools for monitoring IT asset utilization and performance metrics. Students develop skills in using planning software and data analysis techniques to support strategic decision-making. Upon completion, students can design comprehensive IT resource plans that align technical capabilities with organizational objectives and financial constraints.
1269: This course examines the architectural principles and design patterns underlying modern computing platforms, including cloud infrastructure, containerization, and distributed systems. Students learn to deploy and manage applications using technologies such as Docker, Kubernetes, and major cloud providers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud), while understanding virtualization concepts and microservices architecture. The course covers platform scalability, reliability, and security considerations through hands-on projects involving infrastructure-as-code and orchestration tools. 1270: This course covers the installation, configuration, and administration of modern operating systems across Windows, Linux, and Unix environments.
