Through hands-on labs, students develop practical skills in command-line interfaces, shell scripting, system monitoring tools, and troubleshooting common OS-level issues. Upon completion, students are able to deploy operating systems in enterprise environments, manage system resources efficiently, automate administrative tasks, and maintain system security and stability.
1271: This course covers the principles and practices of creating, processing, and delivering multimedia content across digital platforms. Students learn digital image and video processing techniques, audio engineering fundamentals, and compression algorithms while working with industry-standard tools such as Adobe Creative Suite, FFmpeg, and specialized multimedia frameworks. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations in color theory, signal processing, and codec standards, and practical application through hands-on projects involving image editing, video production, and interactive media development. Students develop competency in optimizing multimedia assets for various delivery channels, managing file formats, and integrating multimedia elements into web and application environments. Upon completion, students can design and implement multimedia solutions, troubleshoot technical issues in media production workflows, and apply performance optimization techniques to multimedia applications.
1272: This course equips students with practical skills in diagnosing, troubleshooting, and resolving hardware and software issues in IT environments. Students develop competency in hardware repair, driver installation, and basic network troubleshooting to provide first and second-level technical support. Upon completion, students are prepared to deliver effective technical assistance to end-users and maintain IT infrastructure reliability in organizational settings.
1273: This course examines the principles and practices of securing investments and managing financial assets within organizational contexts. Students study risk assessment methodologies, portfolio management strategies, and compliance frameworks relevant to information technology investments. Students develop competencies in evaluating investment proposals, implementing security controls for financial systems, and managing budgets for technology infrastructure. 1274: This course examines the principles and practices of search engine optimization within the broader context of digital marketing strategy. 1275: This course covers the fundamental and advanced technologies used in modern web development, including HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript for client-side programming. 1276: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of mobile application development across iOS and Android platforms. The course covers essential mobile technologies including networking, data persistence, sensors, and location services, with emphasis on optimizing performance and battery efficiency. Through hands-on projects, students build functional mobile applications, implement responsive layouts, and integrate third-party APIs. Upon completion, students are able to design, develop, and deploy production-ready mobile applications for contemporary smartphones and tablets.
1277: This course covers the principles and practices of integrating disparate systems and components into cohesive software solutions. Students learn enterprise integration patterns, middleware technologies, and API design methodologies while working with tools such as message brokers, service buses, and integration platforms. Through hands-on projects, students develop the ability to architect scalable integration solutions, implement microservices communication, and troubleshoot integration challenges in complex IT environments. Upon completion, students can design and deploy integrated systems that effectively connect legacy applications, cloud services, and modern software components.
1278: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of system administration, configuration, and maintenance across diverse IT environments. Students learn to manage operating systems (Windows Server, Linux), user accounts, permissions, network services, and system security protocols. The course covers practical tools and utilities for monitoring system performance, managing storage, implementing backup strategies, and troubleshooting common infrastructure issues. Through hands-on labs, students develop proficiency in command-line interfaces, scripting for automation, and deploying updates and patches. Upon completion, students are equipped to maintain stable, secure, and efficient IT systems in organizational settings.
1279: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of relational and non-relational database architectures, design principles, and implementation techniques. Students learn to design normalized database schemas, write complex SQL queries, and manage transactions, indexing, and query optimization. The course covers both traditional SQL databases (PostgreSQL, MySQL) and NoSQL systems (MongoDB, Redis), equipping students to select appropriate database technologies for specific application requirements. Through hands-on projects, students develop practical skills in data modeling, database administration, backup/recovery procedures, and performance tuning. Upon completion, students are able to architect scalable databases, implement efficient data retrieval systems, and apply database management best practices in real-world software development environments.
1280: This course examines the mathematical foundations underlying digital computing systems, covering number systems, Boolean algebra, and logic gates. Students learn to analyze and design combinational and sequential logic circuits using truth tables, Karnaugh maps, and algebraic simplification techniques. The course develops proficiency in converting between binary, decimal, hexadecimal, and octal representations, and in applying De Morgan's laws and other Boolean theorems to optimize logical expressions. Through practical exercises, students construct basic digital circuits and understand how arithmetic operations are implemented at the hardware level. Upon completion, students can design simple logic circuits, minimize Boolean functions, and comprehend the fundamental principles that enable computation in digital systems.
1281: This course introduces students to the principles and practices of digital circuit design using combinational and sequential logic. Students learn to analyze and design digital circuits using Boolean algebra, logic gates, multiplexers, decoders, and flip-flops, while gaining proficiency with hardware description languages (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog. The course covers circuit optimization techniques, timing analysis, and practical implementation on field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and programmable logic devices (PLDs). Through laboratory exercises and design projects, students develop the ability to translate functional specifications into working digital circuits and verify designs through simulation and hardware testing. Upon completion, students are prepared to tackle more advanced topics in microprocessor design, embedded systems, and digital signal processing.
1282: This course covers the fundamental principles of digital and analog circuit design, emphasizing practical schematic development and hardware implementation. Students learn to analyze and design electronic circuits using industry-standard tools such as SPICE simulation software and CAD platforms, while mastering circuit theory, component selection, and signal integrity concepts. The course addresses both combinational and sequential logic design, power distribution, and thermal management in computer systems. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in creating detailed schematics, performing circuit simulations, and validating designs before physical implementation. Upon completion, students are capable of designing functional computer hardware schematics, troubleshooting circuit problems, and collaborating effectively with PCB layout engineers in professional engineering environments.
1283: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical techniques for designing digital systems using hardware description languages and modern design tools. Students learn combinational and sequential logic design, finite state machines, and system-level architecture while working with VHDL or Verilog to implement designs on FPGA platforms. The course emphasizes design methodology, including specification, simulation, synthesis, and verification of digital circuits. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in CAD tools, timing analysis, and hardware-software co-design concepts. Upon completion, students are able to design, simulate, and implement complex digital systems and understand the trade-offs between performance, area, and power consumption in modern digital architectures.
1284: This course examines the fundamental principles of computer architecture and organization, covering processor design, instruction set architecture, and memory hierarchies. 109: This course covers fundamental and advanced techniques in combinatorial optimization, focusing on algorithmic approaches to solving discrete optimization problems. Students apply optimization techniques to real-world problems and gain proficiency with optimization software libraries and solvers. 110: This course examines formal methods for defining and analyzing the meaning of programming language constructs through denotational, operational, and axiomatic semantics frameworks. Students study mathematical foundations including domain theory, lambda calculus, and type systems, applying these concepts to reason about program correctness and equivalence. The course covers semantic analysis tools and techniques for proving properties such as soundness, completeness, and termination of language implementations. Through practical exercises, students develop the ability to construct formal semantic definitions for language features, verify compiler correctness, and apply semantic reasoning to optimize and transform programs. Upon completion, students can formally specify programming language behavior and use semantic analysis to solve complex problems in language design and implementation.
111: This course provides a comprehensive study of matrix theory and its applications in discrete mathematics and theoretical informatics. Students examine eigenvalue problems, matrix decompositions (including SVD, QR, and LU factorizations), and spectral analysis techniques essential for algorithm design and complexity analysis. The course covers advanced topics such as matrix norms, conditioning, and perturbation theory, with emphasis on computational aspects and numerical stability. Students develop proficiency in applying matrix methods to solve systems of linear equations, analyze graph structures through adjacency matrices, and optimize algorithmic performance. By completion, students are able to apply sophisticated matrix techniques to theoretical problems in discrete mathematics and implement efficient matrix-based algorithms for computational informatics applications.
112: This course covers the theory and practice of automated design methodologies for Very Large Scale Integration (VLSI) circuits. Students study hardware description languages (HDL), logic synthesis, placement and routing algorithms, and timing analysis techniques essential for modern chip design. The course emphasizes computer-aided design (CAD) tools and their application to optimize circuit performance, power consumption, and area. Through practical projects, students learn to design and simulate complex digital systems, validate designs through formal verification methods, and understand the constraints of physical implementation. Upon completion, students are able to develop efficient VLSI designs using industry-standard automation tools and apply optimization strategies to meet real-world design specifications.
113: This course examines the theoretical foundations of computational complexity and computability, focusing on the classification of problems by their inherent difficulty. Students study recursion theory, the Church-Turing thesis, and formal models of computation including Turing machines, lambda calculus, and register machines. The course covers complexity classes (P, NP, PSPACE, and beyond), reduction techniques, completeness theory, and undecidability results, with emphasis on proving lower bounds and establishing problem hardness. Students develop rigorous mathematical skills in formal proofs and learn to analyze the computational resources required for algorithmic problems. Upon completion, students can classify computational problems by complexity class, construct formal reductions between problems, and apply theoretical results to assess the feasibility of algorithmic solutions.
114: This course covers advanced topics in graph theory with emphasis on structural properties, algorithmic approaches, and modern applications in theoretical computer science. Students study spectral graph theory, extremal graph problems, random graphs, and advanced coloring techniques including chromatic polynomials and list coloring. The course develops proficiency in analyzing graph algorithms, proving structural theorems, and applying graph-theoretic methods to optimization and complexity problems. Through problem sets and theoretical investigations, students gain the ability to model complex computational problems as graph-theoretic structures and develop efficient solutions using advanced techniques such as probabilistic methods and algebraic approaches.
115: This course explores advanced topics in public key cryptography beyond foundational concepts, covering theoretical frameworks and practical implementations of modern cryptographic systems. Students examine elliptic curve cryptography, lattice-based cryptography, and post-quantum cryptographic schemes, analyzing their mathematical foundations and security properties. The course develops competency in cryptanalysis techniques, including attacks on RSA and discrete logarithm problems, and evaluates resistance to quantum computing threats. Through theoretical analysis and computational exercises, students gain the ability to design secure cryptographic protocols, assess cryptosystem vulnerabilities, and implement advanced encryption and digital signature schemes. The two-part structure allows for comprehensive treatment of both classical public key systems and emerging cryptographic paradigms essential for contemporary information security.
116: This course examines the mathematical foundations underlying modern cryptographic systems and their security properties. Students study number-theoretic problems such as integer factorization, discrete logarithm, and elliptic curve cryptography, along with their computational complexity and resistance to known attacks. The course covers cryptanalytic techniques, including differential and linear cryptanalysis, and explores the design principles of symmetric and asymmetric cryptosystems. Students apply mathematical tools from algebra, number theory, and complexity theory to analyze cipher security, evaluate cryptographic protocols, and identify vulnerabilities in real-world implementations. Upon completion, students can assess the mathematical security of cryptographic schemes and contribute to the design of robust cryptographic solutions.
117: This course examines the design and formal verification of control systems using discrete mathematical methods and logical frameworks. Students study synthesis techniques for finite state machines, temporal logic specifications, and model-checking algorithms to ensure system correctness. The course covers Boolean algebra, Mealy and Moore automata, and the application of tools such as NuSMV and SPIN for automated verification and synthesis. Through practical projects, students develop skills in translating informal requirements into formal specifications and generating optimal control logic that satisfies given constraints. Upon completion, students can design provably correct control systems and apply formal methods to complex real-world problems in embedded systems and reactive computing.
118: This course examines computational methods in ring theory, focusing on algorithmic approaches to solving problems in commutative and non-commutative rings. Students study Gröbner bases, polynomial reduction algorithms, and computational techniques for ideal membership, factorization, and solving polynomial systems. The course covers implementations using computer algebra systems such as Macaulay2 or Singular, enabling students to perform symbolic computations on ring-theoretic structures. Upon completion, students can apply algorithmic methods to analyze ring properties, design efficient algorithms for polynomial manipulation, and solve practical problems in computational algebra and cryptography.
119: This course examines computational models and algorithmic approaches for optical character recognition (OCR) and handwriting recognition systems. Students study pattern recognition techniques, feature extraction methods, and machine learning algorithms including neural networks, hidden Markov models, and support vector machines applied to character classification tasks. The course covers preprocessing methods such as image normalization, segmentation, and binarization, alongside evaluation metrics for recognition accuracy and performance optimization. Through practical implementations, students develop end-to-end character recognition systems, analyze algorithmic complexity, and explore applications in document processing and multilingual text recognition. Upon completion, students can design and implement robust character recognition pipelines and evaluate their effectiveness on real-world datasets.
120: This course covers fundamental algorithms and data structures for solving geometric problems computationally. Students study convex hulls, polygon triangulation, point location, range searching, and Voronoi diagrams, with emphasis on algorithmic efficiency and correctness proofs. The course develops proficiency in implementing geometric algorithms in C++ or Python, analyzing their time and space complexity, and applying them to real-world problems in computer graphics, robotics, and spatial databases. Students complete programming assignments that require building robust geometric libraries and solving complex spatial queries. Upon completion, students can design and implement efficient solutions to geometric problems and understand the theoretical foundations underlying computational geometry applications.
121: This course examines formal verification and specification techniques for ensuring software correctness and reliability. Students study temporal logics (LTL, CTL), model checking algorithms, and theorem proving methodologies applied to concurrent and distributed systems. The course covers tools such as SPIN, TLA+, and Coq for formal specification, verification, and proof development. Through practical assignments, students learn to construct formal models of software systems, verify critical properties, and detect design flaws before implementation. Upon completion, students can apply formal methods to validate complex software systems and communicate correctness guarantees using rigorous mathematical frameworks.
122: This course explores foundational and advanced concepts in artificial intelligence within the context of discrete mathematics and theoretical computation. Students study knowledge representation, logical reasoning systems, search algorithms, machine learning fundamentals, and natural language processing techniques. The course covers propositional and first-order logic, constraint satisfaction problems, heuristic search methods, and probabilistic reasoning frameworks. Through practical implementations, students develop proficiency with AI programming languages and tools while analyzing algorithmic complexity and computational decidability. Upon completion, students can design and implement intelligent systems, formalize domain knowledge, and apply theoretical principles to solve complex computational problems.
123: This course examines the mathematical foundations of information theory and its applications to data compression, communication systems, and cryptography. Students study Shannon entropy, mutual information, channel capacity, and the fundamental limits of data transmission and storage. The course covers source coding theorems, channel coding theory, and rate-distortion theory, with emphasis on both theoretical proofs and practical algorithmic implementations. Students develop proficiency in analyzing information-theoretic properties of discrete systems and applying these concepts to solve problems in data compression, error correction, and secure communication. Through problem sets and projects, students learn to compute information-theoretic quantities and design efficient coding schemes for real-world applications.
124: This course examines formal systems for reasoning and computation, covering propositional and first-order logic, proof theory, and model theory. Students study resolution, unification, and automated theorem proving techniques, with practical implementation of logic programming languages such as Prolog. The course explores computational complexity of logical decision problems, including NP-completeness and undecidability results relevant to constraint satisfaction and knowledge representation. Through theoretical analysis and programming assignments, students develop the ability to design logical systems, construct formal proofs, and apply computational logic to solve problems in artificial intelligence and formal verification.

Through problem-solving and theoretical proofs, students develop the ability to model complex discrete problems combinatorially and derive closed-form or asymptotic solutions. Students develop skills in designing approximation algorithms, proving approximation bounds, and understanding inapproximability barriers. Upon completion, students can evaluate the approximability landscape of optimization problems and select appropriate algorithmic strategies for practical computational challenges.

142: This course covers fundamental and advanced techniques in combinatorial optimization, focusing on algorithms for solving discrete optimization problems with applications to real-world systems. 143: This course examines the formal mathematical foundations underlying programming language design and behavior. The course covers lambda calculus, type systems, proof techniques for program correctness, and semantic equivalence. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, students develop the ability to reason about program behavior, verify language properties, and design semantically sound language features for computational modeling applications.
144: This course provides a comprehensive treatment of matrix theory and its computational applications in numerical analysis. Students study advanced topics including matrix decompositions (QR, SVD, eigenvalue decompositions), matrix norms, conditioning and stability analysis, and iterative methods for solving linear systems. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical implementation, with students developing proficiency in MATLAB or Python for matrix computations and numerical experiments. Upon completion, students are able to analyze the numerical stability of algorithms, select appropriate matrix methods for specific computational problems, and apply matrix analysis techniques to mathematical modeling and scientific computing applications.
145: This course covers fundamental and advanced computational algorithms for solving linear algebra problems arising in scientific computing and mathematical modeling. Students study direct and iterative methods for solving linear systems, eigenvalue computations, matrix factorizations (LU, QR, SVD), and numerical stability analysis. The course emphasizes implementation of algorithms using modern programming languages and numerical libraries, with applications to large-scale problems in engineering and physics. Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithmic complexity, convergence rates, and error propagation in finite precision arithmetic. Through practical assignments, students apply these algorithms to real-world computational problems and learn to select appropriate methods based on matrix structure and problem characteristics.
146: This course provides rigorous mathematical foundations for machine learning, covering linear algebra, multivariate calculus, probability theory, and optimization essential for understanding ML algorithms. Students study convex optimization, gradient descent methods, statistical learning theory, and regularization techniques through formal proofs and theoretical analysis. The course examines the mathematical underpinnings of supervised learning, including loss functions, empirical risk minimization, and generalization bounds. Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithm convergence, computational complexity, and the theoretical guarantees of common ML methods. Upon completion, students can rigorously evaluate ML algorithms, derive new optimization techniques, and apply mathematical reasoning to solve complex machine learning problems.
147: This course covers advanced interpolation techniques for functions of multiple variables, including polynomial interpolation, radial basis functions, and spline methods in higher dimensions. Students develop proficiency in constructing and analyzing interpolants that approximate multivariate data, with emphasis on error estimation, convergence properties, and computational efficiency. The course addresses practical challenges such as the curse of dimensionality and explores scattered data interpolation methods essential for real-world applications. Through theoretical analysis and computational implementations, students learn to select appropriate interpolation schemes for specific problem geometries and data distributions. Applications include surface reconstruction, image processing, and solving partial differential equations via meshless methods.
148: This course covers advanced optimization algorithms and their computational implementation for solving complex mathematical and engineering problems. Students study linear and nonlinear programming, convex optimization, gradient-based methods, and metaheuristic approaches including genetic algorithms and simulated annealing. The course emphasizes numerical stability, convergence analysis, and practical algorithm selection for different problem classes. Students develop proficiency in optimization software packages and implement algorithms in Python or MATLAB to solve real-world optimization problems from engineering, economics, and scientific computing. Upon completion, students can formulate optimization problems mathematically, select appropriate solution methods, and evaluate algorithmic performance on large-scale applications.
149: This course covers fundamental and advanced machine learning algorithms within the context of numerical computation and mathematical modeling. Students study supervised learning methods including regression, classification, and ensemble techniques, alongside unsupervised learning approaches such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course emphasizes the mathematical foundations of learning theory, optimization algorithms (gradient descent, stochastic methods), and regularization techniques for model generalization. Students implement algorithms using Python libraries (scikit-learn, TensorFlow) and apply machine learning to solve real-world modeling problems in scientific computing. Upon completion, students can develop predictive models, evaluate their performance rigorously, and integrate machine learning solutions into computational workflows.
150: This course examines the theory and applications of equidistribution in sequences, focusing on how sequences of real numbers become uniformly distributed modulo one. Students study classical results including Weyl's equidistribution criterion, Kronecker's theorem, and van der Corput's difference theorem, along with modern extensions to multidimensional sequences. The course develops computational methods for analyzing distribution properties using discrepancy measures and low-discrepancy sequences such as Halton and Sobol sequences. Students apply equidistribution theory to numerical integration, quasi-Monte Carlo methods, and the construction of optimal sampling schemes for mathematical modeling problems. Through theoretical analysis and computational projects, students gain proficiency in assessing sequence quality and selecting appropriate sequences for high-dimensional numerical approximations.
151: This course provides advanced treatment of functional analysis concepts with direct applications to numerical methods and mathematical modeling. Students study Banach and Hilbert spaces, linear operators, spectral theory, and weak convergence, with emphasis on their role in solving differential equations and optimization problems. The course covers variational formulations, weak solutions, and Sobolev spaces, equipping students with theoretical foundations for finite element methods and other numerical schemes. Through problem sets and computational projects, students develop proficiency in applying functional analysis to construct and analyze numerical algorithms for partial differential equations and inverse problems. By course completion, students can rigorously justify convergence of numerical methods and design solution strategies for complex applied problems in engineering and physics.
152: This course examines the theoretical foundations and computational applications of Euclidean algorithms within the context of public accounting systems and numerical analysis. Students study the mathematical principles underlying greatest common divisor (GCD) calculations, extended Euclidean algorithms, and their implementations in modular arithmetic and cryptographic protocols relevant to financial systems. The course covers algorithm complexity analysis, computational efficiency optimization, and practical applications in accounting verification, audit trail validation, and error-detection mechanisms. Students develop proficiency in implementing these algorithms using computational tools and apply them to solve problems in numerical stability and data integrity within accounting frameworks. Upon completion, students can design and analyze efficient algorithmic solutions for mathematical problems in accounting contexts and evaluate their computational performance characteristics.
153: This course applies numerical methods and mathematical modeling techniques to financial markets and derivative pricing. Students study stochastic calculus, the Black-Scholes model, Monte Carlo simulations, and finite difference methods for solving partial differential equations in finance. The course covers interest rate models, portfolio optimization, and risk management frameworks, with emphasis on computational implementation using programming languages such as Python or C++. Students develop practical skills in calibrating models to market data, pricing exotic derivatives, and conducting sensitivity analysis. Upon completion, students are able to construct and implement quantitative models for financial instruments and apply numerical techniques to solve real-world problems in derivatives trading and risk assessment.
154: This course covers the mathematical foundations and computational theory of spline functions, essential tools in numerical approximation and data interpolation. Students examine B-splines, cubic splines, and smoothing splines, learning their construction, properties, and convergence analysis. The course develops practical skills in implementing spline algorithms for function approximation, curve fitting, and solving differential equations numerically. Students apply spline theory to real-world problems in computer graphics, signal processing, and scientific computing using computational software. Upon completion, students can select appropriate spline methods for specific approximation problems and analyze their accuracy and stability characteristics.
155: This course covers fundamental algorithms and computational techniques for solving problems in discrete geometry, including convex hulls, Voronoi diagrams, Delaunay triangulations, and polygon clipping. Students develop proficiency with geometric data structures, spatial indexing methods, and computational complexity analysis specific to geometric problems. The course emphasizes practical implementation using standard computational geometry libraries and programming environments, with applications to mesh generation, computational topology, and geometric optimization. Through theoretical study and hands-on projects, students learn to design and analyze efficient algorithms for geometric queries, intersection detection, and point location problems. Upon completion, students are equipped to apply discrete geometric methods to real-world problems in computer graphics, finite element analysis, and spatial data processing.
156: This course covers the theory and practice of digital signal processing (DSP) techniques essential for analyzing and manipulating discrete-time signals. Students study fundamental concepts including sampling theory, z-transforms, discrete Fourier transforms (DFT), and filter design methodologies for both finite impulse response (FIR) and infinite impulse response (IIR) systems. The course emphasizes practical implementation using MATLAB and Python, enabling students to develop algorithms for signal filtering, spectral analysis, and real-time processing applications. Upon completion, students can design and analyze digital filters, apply FFT algorithms for efficient computation, and implement DSP solutions for engineering problems in telecommunications, audio processing, and data analysis.
157: This course examines the mathematical frameworks and computational techniques for modeling complex biophysical phenomena, including protein dynamics, cellular signaling, and biomolecular interactions. Students develop proficiency in formulating differential equations, stochastic processes, and partial differential equations that describe biological systems at molecular and cellular scales. The course covers numerical methods for solving nonlinear systems, parameter estimation techniques, and sensitivity analysis using computational tools such as MATLAB and Python. Students apply these methods to construct and validate predictive models of real biophysical systems, analyzing model behavior through simulation and comparing results with experimental data. By course completion, students can design appropriate mathematical models for biophysical problems, implement efficient numerical solutions, and interpret computational results in biological contexts.
158: This course covers the mathematical principles underlying modern computer graphics systems, including linear algebra, affine and projective transformations, and vector calculus applied to 3D space. Students study homogeneous coordinates, matrix representations of geometric transformations, and the mathematical foundations of rendering pipelines, including lighting models and shading equations. The course examines curve and surface representations using Bézier curves, B-splines, and NURBS, along with computational methods for geometric operations such as intersection testing and collision detection. Through practical implementations, students develop proficiency in applying these mathematical concepts to solve real-world graphics problems and optimize computational performance in visualization applications.
159: This course examines theoretical foundations and practical applications of regularization techniques for solving ill-posed problems in numerical analysis and mathematical modeling. Students study Tikhonov regularization, truncated singular value decomposition (TSVD), iterative regularization methods, and parameter selection strategies including the L-curve method and generalized cross-validation. The course covers both linear and nonlinear inverse problems, with emphasis on stabilizing solutions to systems with noisy or incomplete data. Through computational projects, students implement regularization algorithms in MATLAB or Python and apply them to real-world problems in image reconstruction, geophysics, and signal processing. Upon completion, students can diagnose ill-posed problems, select appropriate regularization methods, and develop robust numerical solutions for applications requiring noise-resistant parameter estimation.
160: This course develops students' ability to formulate, analyze, and solve real-world problems using mathematical frameworks and computational techniques. Students learn to construct mathematical models from physical, biological, and engineering systems, translate them into differential equations and discrete systems, and implement numerical solutions using programming languages and scientific computing libraries. The course covers model validation, sensitivity analysis, and parameter estimation methods, with emphasis on understanding the relationship between model assumptions and solution accuracy. Students apply these skills to case studies spanning fluid dynamics, population dynamics, chemical kinetics, and optimization problems, developing proficiency in both theoretical model development and practical computational implementation.
161: This seminar course provides advanced graduate students with a forum to present and critically analyze contemporary research in numerical analysis and mathematical modeling. Students engage with cutting-edge developments in computational methods, discretization techniques, and algorithmic approaches to solving complex differential equations and optimization problems. Participants develop skills in technical presentation, peer review, and scholarly communication while exploring specialized topics such as finite element methods, spectral methods, and adaptive mesh refinement. Through regular seminars featuring both faculty research and student presentations, students strengthen their ability to synthesize literature, identify research gaps, and contribute original insights to their field. The course culminates in students delivering a comprehensive research presentation demonstrating mastery of a specialized topic within numerical analysis or mathematical modeling.
162: Students engage in practical application of numerical analysis and mathematical modelling techniques within professional settings, working on real-world computational problems under expert supervision. The course develops proficiency in implementing numerical algorithms, validating mathematical models against empirical data, and communicating technical findings to interdisciplinary teams. Participants apply advanced computational tools and programming languages to solve complex problems in engineering, physics, or applied mathematics domains. Through structured internship or project-based work, students gain experience in problem formulation, algorithm selection, computational implementation, and results interpretation. Upon completion, students demonstrate competency in translating theoretical knowledge into practical solutions and are prepared for careers in research institutions, industry, or academic positions.
163: Students conduct original research under faculty supervision to develop advanced expertise in numerical analysis and mathematical modelling. The thesis involves formulating a complex problem, selecting or developing appropriate numerical methods, implementing computational solutions, and validating results through theoretical analysis and empirical testing. Students demonstrate mastery of mathematical theory, programming proficiency, and scientific communication by producing a substantial written thesis and presenting findings to the academic community. The work contributes novel insights to the field through rigorous application of numerical techniques to real-world or theoretical problems in applied mathematics, computational science, or engineering.

172: This course examines the application of contemporary information technologies within specialized computing domains relevant to the program's focus. Students explore enterprise software solutions, cloud computing platforms, distributed systems management, and network infrastructure tools used in professional practice. The course covers practical implementation of IT systems for data processing, system administration, cybersecurity protocols, and software deployment methodologies. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in industry-standard tools and platforms while learning to evaluate technology solutions for complex computing environments. Upon completion, students are equipped to integrate advanced IT technologies into professional computing projects and make informed technology selection decisions for organizational systems.
173: This course equips students with systematic approaches to designing and conducting research in computing systems and software development. Students learn research methodologies including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, data collection protocols, and statistical analysis techniques applicable to computer science and engineering domains. The course covers literature review strategies, research ethics, documentation standards, and project management frameworks essential for academic and industrial research. Students develop skills in identifying research gaps, defining research questions, and planning empirical studies or theoretical investigations within their specialization. Upon completion, students are prepared to design rigorous research projects, write research proposals, and execute independent or collaborative research initiatives in computing technologies and software systems.
174: This seminar course examines contemporary challenges and emerging trends in the design, development, and optimization of computing systems, networks, and software architectures. Students engage with recent research publications, industry case studies, and technical innovations in areas such as distributed systems, parallel computing, network protocols, and system performance optimization. Through critical analysis and presentation of current literature, students develop expertise in identifying open problems, evaluating proposed solutions, and understanding the state-of-the-art methodologies in their specialization domain. The course emphasizes the ability to synthesize technical knowledge, communicate complex concepts effectively, and contribute meaningfully to ongoing discussions in the field. Students complete independent research projects or literature reviews that position them to engage with advanced topics in their subsequent thesis work.
175: This course examines fundamental and advanced techniques in combinatorial optimization, focusing on algorithmic approaches to solving discrete optimization problems. Students study classical problems including the traveling salesman problem, maximum flow, matching, and scheduling, alongside their corresponding solution methodologies such as dynamic programming, branch-and-bound, and approximation algorithms. The course covers both exact algorithms and heuristic approaches, with emphasis on computational complexity analysis and NP-completeness theory. Students implement optimization algorithms in practical programming environments and apply them to real-world network design, resource allocation, and system configuration problems relevant to computing systems and networks. Upon completion, students can formulate optimization problems mathematically, select appropriate algorithmic strategies, and develop efficient software solutions for complex discrete optimization challenges.
176: This course examines the formal mathematical foundations underlying programming language design and implementation. Students study denotational semantics, operational semantics, and axiomatic semantics as frameworks for precisely defining language behavior and proving program correctness. The course covers lambda calculus, type systems, and domain theory as essential tools for reasoning about computation and language expressiveness. Through rigorous mathematical analysis, students learn to specify language semantics formally, verify semantic properties, and design type systems that guarantee program safety. Upon completion, students can construct formal semantic models for programming languages, analyze language features mathematically, and apply semantic reasoning to solve problems in language design and program verification.
177: This course provides advanced instruction in Java programming technologies for developing enterprise-scale applications and distributed systems. Students study core Java frameworks, object-oriented design patterns, concurrent programming, and database connectivity through JDBC and ORM technologies. The course covers modern development tools including Maven, Git, and integrated development environments, alongside best practices for code quality and testing frameworks such as JUnit. Upon completion, students are able to design and implement robust, scalable Java applications suitable for complex computing systems and network-based solutions within the program's focus on computing machine development.
178: This course examines type systems and semantic analysis techniques fundamental to modern programming language design and implementation. Students study type theory, type inference algorithms, polymorphism, and subtyping relations, alongside semantic analysis methods including scope resolution, symbol table management, and attribute grammar evaluation. The course covers practical implementation of type checkers and analyzers using tools such as parser generators and abstract syntax tree traversal frameworks. Through programming assignments, students develop type inference engines and semantic analyzers for domain-specific or existing programming languages. Upon completion, students can design sound type systems, implement formal semantic analyses, and apply these concepts to compiler construction and language implementation projects.
179: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical applications of artificial intelligence systems within computational environments. Students study machine learning algorithms, neural networks, natural language processing, and knowledge representation techniques, gaining proficiency in implementing AI solutions using Python, TensorFlow, and PyTorch. The course covers supervised and unsupervised learning methods, deep learning architectures, and optimization techniques essential for developing intelligent systems. Through project-based assignments, students design and deploy AI models for classification, prediction, and decision-making tasks relevant to complex computing systems and networks. Upon completion, students are capable of architecting, implementing, and evaluating AI systems that integrate with modern software and hardware infrastructures.
180: This course covers the theoretical foundations and practical applications of logic programming paradigms, emphasizing Prolog as the primary implementation language. Students learn predicate logic, unification algorithms, resolution-based inference mechanisms, and backtracking search strategies that form the basis of logic programming systems. The course addresses knowledge representation, rule-based problem solving, and constraint handling within logical frameworks. Through hands-on programming assignments, students develop proficiency in writing recursive predicates, managing cut operators, and debugging logical programs. Upon completion, students can design and implement logic-based solutions for symbolic computation, knowledge systems, and automated reasoning problems.
181: This course examines advanced techniques for designing, implementing, and managing complex data structures used in modern computing systems. Students study fundamental and specialized data structures including trees, graphs, hash tables, and heap variants, analyzing their performance characteristics through asymptotic complexity analysis. The course covers practical implementation strategies in contemporary programming languages, emphasizing memory management, cache optimization, and algorithmic efficiency in real-world applications. Students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate data structures for specific computational problems and implementing custom structures to solve complex system design challenges. Through hands-on projects, students apply these concepts to optimize software performance in distributed systems and large-scale data processing environments.
182: This course provides advanced study of matrix theory and its computational applications in modern computing systems. Students examine eigenvalue problems, matrix decompositions (SVD, QR, Cholesky), and numerical stability of matrix algorithms, with emphasis on their implementation in large-scale computational systems. The course covers iterative methods for solving linear systems, matrix perturbation theory, and applications to network analysis and machine learning. Students develop proficiency in MATLAB or Python for implementing efficient matrix computations and analyzing algorithm performance. Upon completion, students can design and optimize matrix-based algorithms for complex computational problems in distributed systems and data-intensive applications.
183: This course examines the architectural principles and operational mechanisms of modern computer networks, with emphasis on the OSI and TCP/IP reference models. Students study network protocols across multiple layers, including physical layer transmission standards, data link layer switching, network layer routing algorithms, and transport layer congestion control mechanisms. The course covers practical protocol implementation using packet analysis tools such as Wireshark, network simulation software, and configuration of real networking equipment. Students develop competency in designing network topologies, troubleshooting protocol-level issues, and analyzing network performance metrics. Upon completion, students can architect scalable networks, implement protocol stacks, and optimize network communication for complex computing systems and distributed applications.
184: This course equips students with comprehensive knowledge and practical skills in software testing methodologies, quality assurance frameworks, and defect management processes. Students learn to design and execute various testing strategies including unit testing, integration testing, system testing, and acceptance testing, while mastering industry-standard testing tools and automation frameworks. The course covers test case design techniques, test data generation, performance testing, and security testing, alongside quality metrics and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) pipeline integration. Students develop proficiency in test automation using popular frameworks and gain hands-on experience with bug tracking systems, test management tools, and quality assurance documentation standards. Upon completion, students are able to establish comprehensive testing strategies, implement automated test suites, evaluate software quality, and lead quality assurance initiatives in complex software systems and networks.
185: This course examines the principles and technologies underlying modern data storage systems and their management within computing infrastructures. Students study database architectures, file systems, storage area networks (SANs), and cloud storage solutions, with emphasis on performance optimization and data consistency. The course covers practical implementation of relational and NoSQL databases, indexing strategies, query optimization, and backup/recovery mechanisms. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in database administration tools, storage virtualization platforms, and data management frameworks. Upon completion, students are capable of designing scalable storage solutions, implementing efficient data management strategies, and troubleshooting storage system performance issues in enterprise computing environments.
186: This course examines advanced techniques for extracting meaningful patterns and knowledge from large datasets using machine learning and statistical methods. Students study supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, including classification, regression, clustering, and dimensionality reduction, with emphasis on their theoretical foundations and practical applications. The course covers feature engineering, model selection, validation strategies, and performance evaluation metrics essential for building robust predictive systems. Students gain hands-on experience implementing algorithms using Python libraries such as scikit-learn, TensorFlow, and pandas, and apply these methods to real-world datasets from various domains. Upon completion, students can design and deploy intelligent data analysis pipelines, select appropriate algorithms for specific problems, and interpret results in the context of complex computing systems and networks.
187: This course examines the principles and practices of designing and implementing parallel and distributed systems. Students study concurrency models, synchronization mechanisms, message-passing architectures, and distributed algorithms while working with modern frameworks such as MPI, OpenMP, and cloud computing platforms. The course covers performance analysis, scalability optimization, fault tolerance, and consistency models in distributed environments. Through practical programming assignments, students develop proficiency in writing efficient parallel code, debugging concurrent systems, and deploying applications across networked computing resources. Upon completion, students can architect scalable solutions for multi-processor systems and distributed computing clusters.
188: This course examines the design, optimization, and practical implementation of knowledge bases within intelligent computing systems. Students study knowledge representation schemes, database normalization techniques, indexing strategies, and query optimization methods to enhance retrieval efficiency and system performance. The course covers both relational and semantic knowledge base architectures, including ontology development and reasoning mechanisms. Through hands-on projects, students implement knowledge bases using contemporary tools and frameworks, applying optimization techniques to real-world datasets and evaluating system scalability. Upon completion, students can architect efficient knowledge bases, diagnose performance bottlenecks, and deploy optimized systems for complex computational applications.
189: This course covers the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of compiler design, including lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, and code generation. Students learn to construct lexers and parsers using tools such as Lex and Yacc, implement symbol tables and type systems, and generate intermediate and target code. The course examines compiler optimization techniques, error handling mechanisms, and runtime environments for various programming languages. Through hands-on projects, students design and build a functional compiler or interpreter for a domain-specific or general-purpose language, applying formal language theory and automata concepts to real-world software development challenges.
190: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical applications of forecasting models in business decision-making and strategic planning. Students learn to develop and implement quantitative forecasting techniques including time series analysis, regression models, exponential smoothing, and machine learning approaches for demand forecasting, financial projections, and market analysis. The course covers model selection criteria, validation methodologies, and performance evaluation metrics to assess forecast accuracy and reliability. Students apply these models to real-world business datasets using statistical software and programming tools, developing the ability to translate business problems into appropriate forecasting frameworks and communicate results to stakeholders. Upon completion, students can design, calibrate, and deploy forecasting systems that support operational and strategic business decisions.
191: This course examines fundamental and advanced cybersecurity principles within information technology infrastructure and systems. Students study cryptographic algorithms, network security protocols, authentication mechanisms, and vulnerability assessment methodologies while analyzing real-world attack vectors and defense strategies. The course covers security architecture design, secure coding practices, penetration testing frameworks, and compliance standards relevant to IT systems and networks. Through hands-on labs and case studies, students develop practical skills in implementing firewalls, intrusion detection systems, encryption technologies, and security incident response procedures. Upon completion, students are equipped to design secure IT systems, conduct security audits, and develop comprehensive cybersecurity strategies for computing complexes and networked environments.
192: This course examines methodologies and technologies for processing, managing, and analyzing large-scale datasets in distributed computing environments. Students learn fundamental concepts of big data architecture, including data storage systems (HDFS, NoSQL databases), processing frameworks (MapReduce, Spark), and stream processing tools. The course covers data preprocessing techniques, statistical analysis methods, and machine learning algorithms optimized for big data contexts. Students develop practical skills in implementing data pipelines, optimizing query performance, and extracting actionable insights from complex datasets using industry-standard tools and platforms. Upon completion, students are capable of designing and executing efficient big data solutions for real-world computational problems in modern computing systems and networks.
193: This course examines mathematical foundations and computational techniques for digital image processing and analysis. Students study linear algebra, Fourier analysis, wavelet transforms, and partial differential equations as applied to image filtering, enhancement, restoration, and segmentation. The course covers convolution operations, frequency domain processing, morphological operations, and edge detection algorithms, with emphasis on both theoretical justification and practical implementation. Students develop proficiency in MATLAB or Python for implementing image processing pipelines and analyzing real-world imaging problems. Upon completion, students can design and implement mathematical models for solving complex image processing tasks in computer vision, medical imaging, and signal analysis applications.
