Students explore key concepts including cultural identity, cultural transmission, and intercultural communication while analyzing diverse cultural systems across historical and contemporary contexts. The course develops critical analytical skills for interpreting cultural artifacts, practices, and institutions through multiple theoretical frameworks drawn from anthropology, sociology, and cultural theory. Participants learn to apply qualitative research methods and comparative analysis techniques to investigate cultural phenomena and their social implications. Upon completion, students are equipped to recognize cultural diversity, engage in informed cross-cultural dialogue, and apply cultural analysis to real-world contexts within their professional and academic pursuits.
220: This course introduces students to core psychological principles and theories that underpin human behavior, cognition, and mental processes. Students examine foundational concepts including perception, learning, memory, motivation, emotion, and personality, with emphasis on empirical research methods and evidence-based findings. The course covers major psychological perspectives—biological, cognitive, behavioral, and social—and their applications to real-world contexts. Through case studies and practical examples, students develop critical thinking skills for analyzing psychological phenomena and understanding individual differences. This foundational knowledge prepares students to apply psychological insights in professional contexts, particularly relevant for those pursuing careers in human-computer interaction, user experience design, or data-driven decision-making in applied mathematics.
221: This course introduces students to the foundational principles of mathematical logic and formal reasoning. Students learn propositional logic, predicate logic, logical inference rules, and methods for constructing formal proofs. The course covers truth tables, logical equivalences, quantifiers, and techniques for translating natural language statements into formal logical notation. Through problem-solving exercises, students develop the ability to analyze logical arguments, identify fallacies, and apply logical reasoning to computational problems and algorithm design.
222: This course examines foundational ethical theories and their applications to contemporary issues in technology and computing. Students explore classical philosophical frameworks including deontology, consequentialism, and virtue ethics, alongside modern approaches to digital ethics, data privacy, and algorithmic responsibility. The course develops critical thinking skills for analyzing ethical dilemmas in software development, artificial intelligence, and information systems. Through case studies and discussions, students learn to identify stakeholders, evaluate competing values, and construct reasoned ethical arguments relevant to their work as informaticians and applied mathematicians. Upon completion, students can apply ethical reasoning to real-world computing problems and communicate their positions on technology ethics to technical and non-technical audiences.
223: This course introduces students to core sociological concepts, theories, and research methodologies essential for understanding human society and social structures. Students examine classical and contemporary sociological perspectives, including functionalism, conflict theory, and symbolic interactionism, while analyzing key social institutions such as family, education, economy, and politics. The course develops students' ability to apply sociological imagination to real-world social phenomena and critically evaluate social issues through empirical evidence and theoretical frameworks. Students gain practical skills in qualitative and quantitative research design, data interpretation, and social analysis relevant to applied mathematics and informatics contexts. By course completion, students can identify sociological patterns in data, understand social dimensions of technology adoption, and communicate sociological insights to interdisciplinary audiences.
224: This course examines fundamental principles and contemporary developments across physics, chemistry, and biology that underpin modern scientific understanding. Students explore quantum mechanics, molecular structure, thermodynamics, and evolutionary biology while analyzing how these concepts interconnect within complex systems. The course emphasizes the mathematical and computational frameworks used to model natural phenomena, including differential equations, statistical methods, and simulation techniques. Through case studies and problem-solving exercises, students develop the ability to apply scientific reasoning to real-world phenomena and evaluate emerging research in their respective fields. The course prepares students to integrate scientific knowledge with computational approaches essential for careers in applied mathematics and informatics.
225: This course covers fundamental and applied statistical methods essential for data analysis and decision-making in real-world contexts. Students learn probability theory, descriptive statistics, hypothesis testing, regression analysis, and experimental design, with emphasis on practical applications across engineering, economics, and natural sciences. The course develops proficiency in statistical software packages (such as R or Python) for data manipulation, visualization, and computational analysis. Students apply statistical techniques to analyze datasets, interpret results critically, and communicate findings through technical reports. Upon completion, students are equipped to design experiments, conduct statistical inference, and solve applied problems using quantitative methods.
226: This course introduces students to the foundational principles of law and legal systems relevant to modern society. Students examine constitutional law, civil law, criminal law, and administrative law, gaining understanding of how legal frameworks govern individual rights, business operations, and state functions. The course develops students' ability to interpret legal documents, understand contractual obligations, and recognize legal implications in professional contexts. Through case analysis and practical examples, students learn to apply legal reasoning to real-world scenarios they may encounter in technical and business environments. This foundation prepares informatics and applied mathematics professionals to navigate legal considerations in software development, data protection, intellectual property, and technology-related business practices.
227: This course develops students' analytical and innovative problem-solving capabilities through systematic examination of logical reasoning, argumentation, and cognitive biases. Students learn to evaluate information sources, identify fallacies, and construct sound arguments while applying creative techniques such as brainstorming, lateral thinking, and design thinking methodologies. The course emphasizes practical applications across mathematical, computational, and real-world contexts, enabling students to approach complex problems from multiple perspectives. Through case studies and collaborative exercises, students practice decomposing problems, generating novel solutions, and communicating their reasoning effectively. Upon completion, students will be equipped to think critically about technical challenges and apply structured creative approaches to research and professional work in informatics and applied mathematics.
228: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for part-time informatics and applied mathematics students. Students engage with technical and academic Russian texts, including scientific articles, documentation, and professional communications relevant to their field of study. The course emphasizes reading comprehension, written expression, and oral communication in formal academic and professional contexts. Students practice translating specialized terminology, writing technical reports, and participating in discussions on complex topics. Upon completion, students demonstrate the ability to comprehend and produce advanced-level Russian in academic and professional settings.
229: This course develops advanced English language proficiency for informatics and applied mathematics students through specialized technical and academic communication. Students engage with discipline-specific texts, including research papers, technical documentation, and scientific articles relevant to computer science and mathematics. The course emphasizes reading comprehension, academic writing, and oral presentation skills tailored to professional and scholarly contexts in STEM fields. Students practice writing technical reports, abstracts, and research proposals while expanding vocabulary in mathematics and computer science terminology. Upon completion, students will be able to comprehend complex technical English texts, communicate research findings effectively in written and oral formats, and participate confidently in international academic and professional environments.
230: This course develops students' analytical and innovative problem-solving capabilities through systematic study of logical reasoning, argumentation, and creative ideation techniques. Students examine formal and informal logic, evaluate evidence quality, identify cognitive biases, and construct sound arguments across technical and non-technical domains. The course integrates critical analysis frameworks with creative methodologies such as lateral thinking, brainstorming, and design thinking to enable students to approach complex problems from multiple perspectives. Through case studies and practical exercises, students learn to synthesize information, challenge assumptions, and generate novel solutions applicable to informatics and applied mathematics research. Upon completion, students will be equipped to evaluate claims rigorously, construct well-reasoned arguments, and apply structured creative processes to academic and professional challenges.
231: This course develops students' analytical and innovative problem-solving capabilities through systematic examination of logical reasoning, argumentation, and creative ideation techniques. Students learn to evaluate information sources, identify cognitive biases, construct sound arguments, and apply structured methodologies such as design thinking and lateral thinking to complex problems. The course emphasizes practical application across technical and non-technical domains, enabling students to deconstruct problems, generate multiple solution pathways, and synthesize creative approaches with rigorous analytical frameworks. Through case studies and collaborative exercises, students practice critical evaluation of assumptions, evidence assessment, and the formulation of well-reasoned conclusions. Upon completion, students will be equipped to approach professional challenges with enhanced analytical rigor and creative flexibility, essential competencies for advanced work in informatics and applied mathematics.
232: This course introduces students to core business principles and organizational management within the context of technology and applied mathematics. Students examine fundamental concepts including business strategy, financial management, marketing, and operations while exploring their application in IT and software enterprises. The course develops practical skills in business analysis, financial literacy, and project management relevant to technology professionals. Through case studies and real-world scenarios, students learn to evaluate business decisions, understand market dynamics, and communicate technical concepts to non-technical stakeholders. Upon completion, students are equipped to transition into business-oriented roles or manage technical projects with awareness of broader organizational objectives.
233: This course introduces students to fundamental economic principles and their applications to real-world problems. Students examine microeconomic concepts including supply and demand, consumer behavior, production theory, and market structures, alongside macroeconomic topics such as national income accounting, inflation, unemployment, and monetary and fiscal policy. The course develops analytical skills in quantitative economic modeling, enabling students to interpret economic data and construct basic econometric models using spreadsheet software and statistical tools. Through case studies and problem sets, students apply economic reasoning to business decisions, resource allocation, and policy analysis. Upon completion, students will be able to analyze economic phenomena using graphical and mathematical models and evaluate the economic implications of business and policy decisions.
234: This course extends foundational calculus concepts to multivariable functions and their applications. Students study partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and differential equations, developing proficiency in analyzing functions of several variables. The course emphasizes computational techniques and theoretical foundations necessary for advanced mathematics and applied sciences. Students learn to solve optimization problems, evaluate line and surface integrals, and apply calculus to real-world modeling scenarios in physics and engineering. Upon completion, students can manipulate multivariable functions, construct and solve differential equations, and apply vector calculus methods to complex problems.
235: This course covers fundamental and advanced optimization techniques essential for solving real-world computational problems. Students study linear programming, nonlinear optimization, convex analysis, and integer programming, learning both theoretical foundations and practical algorithmic approaches including the simplex method, gradient descent, and branch-and-bound algorithms. The course emphasizes formulating optimization problems mathematically and selecting appropriate solution methods based on problem structure and constraints. Through practical assignments, students implement optimization algorithms using standard software tools and apply them to engineering, economics, and data science applications. Upon completion, students can model complex optimization problems, analyze algorithm convergence properties, and develop efficient computational solutions for constrained and unconstrained optimization scenarios.
236: This course examines the design, analysis, and optimization of combinatorial algorithms with emphasis on computational complexity and practical efficiency. Students study fundamental algorithmic paradigms including greedy methods, dynamic programming, and backtracking, alongside formal techniques for time and space complexity analysis using Big-O notation and recurrence relations. The course covers classical problems such as sorting, graph traversal, shortest paths, and optimization on discrete structures, with rigorous proofs of algorithm correctness and complexity bounds. Students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate algorithms for specific problem classes and implementing solutions in standard programming languages while evaluating trade-offs between solution quality and computational resources. By course completion, students can analyze algorithmic performance theoretically and empirically, recognize NP-complete problems, and apply algorithmic techniques to solve real-world computational challenges.
237: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and practical applications of data science within the context of modern information systems. Students learn statistical analysis, machine learning algorithms, and data visualization techniques using industry-standard tools such as Python, R, and SQL for data manipulation and analysis. The curriculum covers data preprocessing, exploratory data analysis, predictive modeling, and evaluation metrics essential for extracting actionable insights from large datasets. Through hands-on projects and case studies, students develop the ability to design data pipelines, build and validate machine learning models, and communicate findings to both technical and non-technical audiences. Upon completion, students are equipped to tackle real-world data problems and contribute to data-driven decision-making in various organizational contexts.
238: This course examines the fundamental principles of algorithm design, analysis, and complexity theory. Students study algorithmic paradigms including divide-and-conquer, dynamic programming, greedy algorithms, and graph algorithms, alongside formal methods for analyzing time and space complexity using Big-O notation. The course covers essential data structures and their applications, enabling students to evaluate algorithm efficiency and select appropriate solutions for computational problems. Through problem-solving exercises and implementation projects, students develop the ability to design efficient algorithms, prove their correctness, and apply complexity analysis to real-world computational challenges.
239: This course covers the theory and applications of partial differential equations (PDEs) that model physical phenomena. Students study the classification of PDEs (elliptic, parabolic, and hyperbolic types), boundary value problems, and initial value problems, with emphasis on the heat equation, wave equation, and Laplace equation. The course develops analytical solution techniques including separation of variables, Fourier series, and integral transforms (Laplace and Fourier transforms). Students apply these methods to solve real-world problems in heat conduction, wave propagation, and potential theory, and gain proficiency in both theoretical analysis and computational verification of solutions.
240: This course covers the theory and methods for solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs), fundamental to modeling dynamic systems in science and engineering. Students study first-order equations, higher-order linear equations, systems of differential equations, and qualitative analysis techniques including phase plane analysis and stability theory. The course develops proficiency in analytical solution methods (separation of variables, integrating factors, variation of parameters) and numerical approximation techniques for problems lacking closed-form solutions. Students apply ODEs to real-world problems in physics, biology, and engineering, learning to formulate differential equation models and interpret their solutions in practical contexts. Upon completion, students can classify differential equations, select appropriate solution methods, and analyze the behavior of dynamic systems.
241: This course examines mathematical methods and algorithms for optimizing decision-making in complex systems. Students study linear programming, integer programming, network flow problems, and dynamic programming, applying simplex methods and branch-and-bound techniques to real-world operational challenges. The course covers formulation of optimization models, sensitivity analysis, and computational approaches using standard OR software tools. Students develop proficiency in problem modeling, solution implementation, and interpretation of results for applications in logistics, resource allocation, and production planning. Upon completion, students can formulate optimization problems, select appropriate solution methods, and implement solutions using computational tools.
242: This course covers fundamental numerical techniques for solving linear algebraic problems arising in scientific and engineering applications. Students learn direct methods (Gaussian elimination, LU decomposition, QR factorization) and iterative methods (Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, conjugate gradient) for solving systems of linear equations, along with algorithms for eigenvalue and eigenvector computation. The course emphasizes computational stability, error analysis, and algorithmic complexity, with practical implementation in programming languages such as Python or MATLAB. Students develop proficiency in selecting appropriate numerical methods based on matrix properties and problem constraints, and apply these techniques to solve real-world problems in physics, engineering, and data analysis.
243: This course covers the theory and applications of complex-valued functions, including complex differentiation, analytic functions, and the Cauchy-Riemann equations. Students study contour integration, residue theory, and conformal mappings, developing proficiency in evaluating complex integrals and solving boundary value problems. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical computational techniques, enabling students to apply complex analysis to problems in physics, engineering, and applied mathematics. Through problem sets and examinations, students demonstrate mastery of singularity classification, Laurent series expansions, and the residue theorem for evaluating real integrals.
244: This course covers fundamental data structures essential for efficient algorithm design and software development. Students study arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, analyzing their properties, operations, and performance characteristics using Big O notation. Through practical programming assignments in C++ or Java, students implement these structures from scratch and apply them to solve computational problems. The course emphasizes choosing appropriate data structures for specific applications and understanding trade-offs between time and space complexity. Upon completion, students can design efficient algorithms, optimize code performance, and tackle complex programming challenges in their professional practice.
245: This course introduces students to fundamental machine learning concepts, algorithms, and applications within the context of data-driven problem solving. Students learn supervised learning techniques including regression, classification, and ensemble methods, alongside unsupervised learning approaches such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course covers essential tools and libraries including Python, scikit-learn, and TensorFlow, enabling students to implement algorithms from scratch and utilize established frameworks. Students develop practical skills in data preprocessing, feature engineering, model evaluation, and hyperparameter tuning through hands-on projects. By course completion, students can build, train, and deploy machine learning models to solve real-world classification and prediction problems while understanding the theoretical foundations underlying these techniques.
246: This course covers the foundational principles of mathematical logic, including propositional logic, first-order predicate logic, and formal proof systems. Students learn to construct and analyze logical formulas, apply inference rules, and evaluate the validity of arguments using truth tables, natural deduction, and resolution methods. The course examines key concepts such as satisfiability, completeness, and decidability, with emphasis on their applications in computer science and automated reasoning. Through problem-solving exercises, students develop the ability to formalize mathematical statements, design logical proofs, and understand the theoretical limitations of formal systems. This foundation prepares students for advanced work in computational logic, formal verification, and theoretical computer science.
247: This course introduces students to the foundational concepts of mathematical analysis, covering limits, continuity, and differentiation of single-variable functions. Students develop rigorous understanding of real numbers, sequences, and series, learning to construct formal proofs and apply epsilon-delta definitions. The course emphasizes computational techniques including derivatives, optimization, and applications to real-world problems in physics and engineering. By completion, students can analyze function behavior, solve differential equations, and apply calculus methods to model and solve applied mathematics problems.
248: This course covers advanced topics in mathematical analysis including sequences and series of functions, uniform convergence, power series, and Fourier series. Students develop rigorous proofs of convergence theorems and learn techniques for analyzing the behavior of complex functions. The course emphasizes applications to differential equations and approximation theory, equipping students with analytical tools essential for advanced mathematics and computational work. By completion, students can determine convergence properties of function sequences, manipulate power series expansions, and apply Fourier analysis to solve practical problems in applied mathematics and engineering.
249: This course covers fundamental and advanced concepts in graph theory, including graph representations, connectivity, paths, cycles, and tree structures. Students learn to analyze graph properties using adjacency matrices, adjacency lists, and incidence matrices, and apply classical algorithms such as depth-first search, breadth-first search, and shortest path computations. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations—including planarity, coloring problems, and matching theory—and practical problem-solving through implementation of graph algorithms in programming languages. By course completion, students can model real-world problems as graphs, select appropriate algorithmic approaches for specific graph problems, and implement efficient solutions for applications in network analysis, optimization, and computer science.
250: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles and architecture of computer networks. Students study the OSI and TCP/IP reference models, network protocols, IP addressing, routing algorithms, and data link layer technologies including Ethernet and wireless standards. The course covers practical networking tools such as packet analyzers (Wireshark), network configuration utilities, and command-line diagnostics to analyze network traffic and troubleshoot connectivity issues. Through hands-on exercises, students configure network devices, implement basic routing and switching concepts, and design simple network topologies. Upon completion, students can design basic network architectures, analyze network performance, and apply foundational networking knowledge to real-world infrastructure problems.
251: This course covers the foundational concepts of differential calculus essential for applied mathematics and computer science. Students study limits, continuity, derivatives, and their applications to optimization and curve analysis. The course develops computational skills in differentiation techniques, including the chain rule, product rule, and implicit differentiation, with emphasis on solving real-world problems in physics and engineering. Through problem-solving exercises and applications, students learn to analyze function behavior and construct mathematical models for practical phenomena. Upon completion, students are able to compute derivatives, apply calculus to optimization problems, and understand the theoretical foundations necessary for advanced mathematics courses.
252: Mathematical Analysis - 3 develops students' understanding of multivariable calculus and advanced analytical techniques essential for applied mathematics and computer science. The course covers partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and differential forms, with emphasis on rigorous proofs and computational methods. Students learn to analyze functions of several variables, solve optimization problems, and apply Green's, Stokes', and divergence theorems to physical and engineering problems. Through problem sets and practical exercises, students develop proficiency in computing line and surface integrals, understanding vector fields, and applying analytical methods to real-world applications in informatics and applied mathematics.
253: This course covers advanced topics in discrete mathematics essential for computer science and applied mathematics. Students study graph theory, including trees, connectivity, and algorithms for shortest paths and minimum spanning trees; combinatorics with emphasis on permutations, combinations, and recurrence relations; and Boolean algebra with applications to digital logic design. Through problem-solving sessions and computational exercises, students develop proficiency in mathematical proof techniques, algorithm analysis, and discrete optimization methods. Upon completion, students can model computational problems using discrete structures, analyze algorithm complexity, and apply combinatorial reasoning to real-world informatics challenges.
254: Programming - 2 builds on foundational programming concepts to develop advanced problem-solving skills using object-oriented and functional programming paradigms. Students master data structures including trees, graphs, and hash tables, implementing efficient algorithms for sorting, searching, and graph traversal. The course covers memory management, recursion, and design patterns while utilizing industry-standard development tools and version control systems. Through practical assignments and projects, students develop the ability to write scalable, maintainable code and analyze algorithmic complexity using Big O notation. Upon completion, students can design and implement complex software solutions, debug efficiently, and apply appropriate data structures to optimize program performance.
255: This course covers the fundamentals of web application development using modern programming languages and frameworks. Students learn front-end technologies including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, alongside back-end development with server-side languages such as Python or PHP. The course emphasizes practical skills in database design, RESTful API development, and version control systems, with hands-on projects building full-stack web applications. By course completion, students are able to design and implement dynamic websites, manage client-server interactions, and deploy web applications to production environments.
256: Mathematical Analysis - 2 continues the study of single-variable calculus with emphasis on integration theory, sequences, and series. Students master techniques of indefinite and definite integration, including substitution and integration by parts, and develop rigorous understanding of convergence criteria for infinite series and power series expansions. The course covers applications of integration to computing areas, volumes, and arc lengths, alongside the theoretical foundations of limits and continuity in the context of real analysis. Upon completion, students are able to solve complex integration problems, analyze the convergence behavior of sequences and series, and apply analytical methods to model and solve applied mathematics problems.
257: This course introduces fundamental programming concepts and practices using a modern programming language. Students learn core programming constructs including variables, data types, control flow, functions, and basic data structures such as arrays and strings. The course emphasizes problem-solving methodology and algorithmic thinking through hands-on coding exercises and projects. Upon completion, students are able to write, debug, and test simple programs, implement basic algorithms, and apply structured programming principles to solve computational problems.
258: This course covers fundamental mathematical concepts and analytical geometry essential for applied mathematics and computer science applications. Students study vector algebra, coordinate systems, curves and surfaces in two and three dimensions, and the geometric interpretation of algebraic equations. The course develops proficiency in solving systems of linear equations, analyzing conic sections, and applying vector methods to geometric problems. Through problem-solving exercises and computational work, students gain the ability to model spatial relationships mathematically and apply geometric reasoning to real-world applications in informatics and applied mathematics.
259: This course introduces fundamental concepts in discrete mathematics essential for computer science and applied mathematics. Students study set theory, logic, combinatorics, graph theory basics, and mathematical proofs, developing rigorous reasoning skills required for algorithm design and analysis. The course emphasizes problem-solving techniques including counting principles, permutations, combinations, and logical inference methods. Through practical exercises and theoretical work, students learn to construct formal proofs and apply discrete structures to computational problems. Upon completion, students can analyze algorithmic complexity, model computational problems using graphs and sets, and apply combinatorial reasoning to real-world informatics challenges.
260: This course teaches students to design and develop graphical user interfaces using modern frameworks and libraries. Students learn fundamental GUI concepts including event handling, layout management, component hierarchies, and user interaction patterns across desktop and web platforms. The course covers practical implementation using industry-standard tools such as Qt, JavaFX, or web-based frameworks, with emphasis on responsive design and accessibility principles. Through hands-on projects, students develop the ability to create functional, user-centered applications that integrate backend logic with intuitive frontend interfaces. By course completion, students can architect GUI applications, implement complex interactive features, and apply software engineering best practices to interface development.
261: This course examines the theoretical foundations of translation as both a linguistic and cultural practice, with emphasis on computational and mathematical approaches to translation problems. Students study major translation theories including equivalence-based, functionalist, and corpus-based approaches, alongside formal models of semantic transfer and language mapping. The course covers practical applications in machine translation, multilingual natural language processing, and automated terminology management, utilizing tools such as translation memory systems and statistical translation models. Students develop skills in analyzing translation quality, identifying linguistic divergences between language pairs, and applying algorithmic methods to translation challenges. By course completion, students are able to critically evaluate translation theories, design translation workflows for specialized domains, and implement computational solutions to translation problems.
262: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations and computational techniques of digital signal and data analysis. Students learn discrete mathematics concepts, Fourier analysis, wavelet transforms, and statistical methods for processing digital signals and time-series data. The course covers practical implementation using programming languages and specialized software tools for signal filtering, feature extraction, and pattern recognition. Students develop proficiency in analyzing real-world datasets, interpreting frequency-domain representations, and applying computational algorithms to solve problems in engineering and applied mathematics. Upon completion, students are able to preprocess digital data, perform spectral analysis, and implement signal processing pipelines for practical applications.
263: This course examines the application of mathematical modeling and analysis techniques to solve problems in physics, chemistry, and biology. Students learn to formulate natural phenomena as mathematical equations, including differential equations, partial differential equations, and systems of equations, and develop proficiency in both analytical and numerical solution methods. The course covers dimensional analysis, scaling arguments, and perturbation theory as tools for simplifying complex systems and extracting essential physical insights. Through practical problem-solving sessions, students apply these mathematical frameworks to real-world scenarios such as population dynamics, chemical kinetics, and fluid mechanics. Upon completion, students are able to translate scientific problems into mathematical language and select appropriate analytical or computational approaches for their solution.
264: This course covers fundamental data structures essential for efficient algorithm design and software development. Students learn the implementation and analysis of arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, trees, graphs, and hash tables, examining time and space complexity for each structure. The course emphasizes practical programming in C++ or Python, requiring students to implement data structures from scratch and apply them to solve computational problems. Students develop the ability to select appropriate data structures for specific applications, optimize code performance, and analyze algorithmic efficiency using Big O notation. By course completion, students can design and implement complex data structure solutions for real-world programming challenges encountered in software engineering and computer science applications.
265: This course examines the fundamental principles of computer architecture, including CPU design, memory hierarchies, instruction sets, and data representation at the hardware level. Students learn x86-64 assembly language programming, mastering low-level operations such as register manipulation, memory addressing modes, control flow, and function calls. Through practical programming assignments, students develop proficiency in writing, debugging, and optimizing assembly code while understanding how high-level language constructs map to machine instructions. The course covers interrupt handling, I/O operations, and system-level programming concepts essential for systems development. Upon completion, students can analyze processor behavior, write efficient assembly programs, and comprehend the interface between software and hardware architecture.
266: This course provides students with a rigorous foundation in functional analysis, examining infinite-dimensional vector spaces and linear operators. Students study Banach spaces, Hilbert spaces, and their fundamental properties, including completeness, compactness, and spectral theory. The course covers key theorems such as the Hahn-Banach theorem, open mapping theorem, and closed graph theorem, with applications to differential and integral equations. Through problem-solving and theoretical exercises, students develop the ability to analyze functional equations, prove convergence properties, and apply functional analytic methods to solve applied mathematics problems in optimization and numerical analysis.
267: This course examines the qualitative behavior of solutions to differential equations without requiring explicit analytical solutions. Students study phase plane analysis, stability theory, and bifurcation phenomena to understand long-term dynamics of nonlinear systems. The course covers equilibrium points, limit cycles, Lyapunov stability, and the classification of critical points using eigenvalue analysis. Students apply these techniques to model and analyze real-world phenomena in physics, biology, and engineering, developing the ability to predict system behavior and determine stability without solving equations explicitly. Computational tools and graphical methods are employed to visualize phase portraits and validate theoretical predictions.
268: This course covers fundamental and advanced combinatorial algorithms essential for solving discrete optimization problems. Students study graph algorithms, dynamic programming techniques, greedy methods, and backtracking approaches, with emphasis on analyzing time and space complexity. The course includes practical implementation of algorithms for problems such as shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, matching, and constraint satisfaction. Students develop proficiency in algorithm design, correctness proofs, and performance optimization using standard programming languages. Upon completion, students can select appropriate algorithmic strategies for combinatorial problems, implement efficient solutions, and evaluate algorithmic trade-offs in real-world applications.
269: This course covers fundamental and advanced algorithms for solving graph-theoretic problems essential to computer science and discrete mathematics. Students study classical algorithms including depth-first search, breadth-first search, shortest path algorithms (Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford), minimum spanning trees (Kruskal, Prim), and topological sorting, along with their correctness proofs and complexity analysis. The course emphasizes practical implementation of graph data structures and algorithms in programming languages, with applications to network analysis, optimization problems, and real-world computational challenges. Students develop proficiency in analyzing algorithm efficiency, selecting appropriate algorithms for specific problem contexts, and implementing solutions to graph-based problems in software projects.
270: Students engage in supervised practical work within industry or research organizations, applying theoretical knowledge from their informatics and applied mathematics coursework to real-world problems. The course develops professional competencies in software development, data analysis, algorithm implementation, and mathematical modeling through direct project involvement. Participants gain hands-on experience with industry-standard tools, version control systems, and collaborative development practices while working under the guidance of experienced practitioners. Upon completion, students demonstrate the ability to translate academic concepts into functional solutions, document technical work professionally, and integrate effectively within technical teams. This practice-based learning bridges the gap between classroom instruction and career-ready expertise in computing and applied mathematics.
271: This course introduces students to the mathematical foundations of cybernetics, focusing on control systems, information theory, and decision-making processes. Students study automata theory, formal languages, Boolean algebra, and graph theory as tools for modeling complex systems. The course covers feedback mechanisms, stability analysis, and optimization techniques essential for designing and analyzing automated control systems. Through problem-solving and theoretical exercises, students develop the ability to formalize real-world problems using cybernetic models and apply mathematical methods to solve them. Upon completion, students can analyze system behavior, design simple control algorithms, and apply cybernetic principles to information processing and computational problems.
272: This course examines advanced methodologies and theoretical frameworks in action research, emphasizing practical application within computational and mathematical contexts. Students explore the design, implementation, and evaluation of action research projects, learning to integrate empirical investigation with iterative problem-solving in real-world informatics scenarios. The course covers data collection techniques, qualitative and quantitative analysis methods, and strategies for translating research findings into actionable improvements in software development and mathematical modeling. Students develop competency in documenting research processes, managing research cycles, and communicating results to both technical and non-technical audiences. By course completion, students will be capable of conducting independent action research projects that address contemporary challenges in applied mathematics and computer science.
273: This course develops students' proficiency in modern Armenian language and effective communication skills within academic and professional contexts. Students study grammar, syntax, and vocabulary essential for technical writing and formal discourse, with emphasis on precision and clarity in expressing complex ideas. The course covers oral presentation techniques, argumentation, and professional communication standards required in information security and technology fields. Through written assignments and oral exercises, students strengthen their ability to communicate security concepts, research findings, and technical documentation in Armenian. By course completion, students can produce well-structured academic texts and deliver professional presentations in Armenian with appropriate terminology and register.
274: This course examines fundamental philosophical concepts and methodologies essential for developing critical thinking in information security contexts. Students engage with epistemology, logic, and ethics to understand knowledge validation, reasoning structures, and moral frameworks governing cybersecurity practices and policy decisions. The course explores philosophical foundations of privacy, autonomy, and justice as they apply to data protection and digital rights. Through analysis of classical and contemporary philosophical texts, students develop analytical skills for evaluating complex security dilemmas and constructing reasoned arguments in professional and academic discourse. Students will be able to apply philosophical reasoning to assess the ethical implications of security technologies and justify security policies through rigorous logical argumentation.
275: This course examines the foundational principles of ecology and environmental protection systems relevant to information security infrastructure and sustainable practices. Students study ecosystem dynamics, environmental regulations, and the ecological impact of data centers and IT operations, including energy consumption and electronic waste management. The course covers environmental monitoring technologies, green computing practices, and compliance frameworks such as ISO 14001 for environmental management systems. Through practical applications, students learn to assess and mitigate the environmental footprint of information security operations and develop sustainable approaches to IT infrastructure deployment. Upon completion, students will be able to evaluate environmental risks associated with cybersecurity systems and implement environmentally responsible security solutions.
276: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for information security students, building upon foundational skills with emphasis on technical and professional communication. Students engage with specialized vocabulary related to cybersecurity, network administration, and information protection systems commonly used in Russian-language technical documentation and professional contexts. The course covers complex grammatical structures, academic writing conventions, and oral presentation skills necessary for reading security research papers, understanding Russian security standards, and communicating with international colleagues in the field. Students practice translating technical security documents, writing formal reports, and participating in professional discussions relevant to their discipline. Upon completion, students demonstrate intermediate-to-advanced Russian language competency with the ability to comprehend and produce specialized security-related content in professional settings.
277: This course examines the political, social, and cultural developments of Armenia from the medieval period through the modern era, with emphasis on the formation of Armenian national identity and statehood. Students analyze primary and secondary sources to understand key historical events, including the establishment of the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia, Ottoman and Persian rule, Russian imperial expansion, and the creation of the Armenian Soviet Socialist Republic. The course develops critical thinking and historical analysis skills through seminar discussions, written assignments, and comparative study of Armenian history within broader regional and global contexts. Students gain foundational knowledge of Armenia's geopolitical position and historical experiences that inform contemporary security and political issues relevant to their information security studies.
278: This course examines the political, social, and cultural development of Armenia from ancient times through the medieval period. Students analyze primary historical sources and archaeological evidence to understand the formation of Armenian identity, the development of the Armenian alphabet, and Armenia's interactions with neighboring empires. By course completion, students can produce coherent written work and deliver presentations on specialized topics with appropriate terminology and rhetorical precision.

544: This course equips students with essential knowledge and practical skills for responding to emergency situations and providing immediate medical assistance. 545: This course examines ethical frameworks and their application to emerging technologies in physics and artificial intelligence. Through case studies and discussions, students develop the ability to identify ethical implications in their research and make principled decisions in technology development. The course prepares students to navigate the ethical dimensions of their future work in physics and AI-related fields.
546: This course examines fundamental principles and recent developments across physics, chemistry, and biology that underpin modern scientific understanding. Students explore quantum mechanics, relativity, thermodynamics, molecular structure, and evolutionary biology while analyzing how these concepts integrate with computational and data-driven approaches. The course emphasizes the mathematical frameworks and experimental methodologies that validate scientific theories, with particular attention to applications in artificial intelligence and data processing. Students develop critical thinking skills in evaluating scientific evidence and understanding how classical and contemporary concepts inform technological innovation. Through case studies and problem-solving exercises, students connect theoretical knowledge to practical applications in their specialized program.
547: This course introduces students to core business principles and practices relevant to technology-driven enterprises and AI applications. 548: This course introduces students to the foundational principles of law and legal systems relevant to technology, data processing, and artificial intelligence applications. 549: This course provides students with practical statistical methods essential for analyzing experimental and computational data in physics and machine learning applications. Students apply these statistical tools to real datasets from physics experiments and AI applications, developing proficiency in exploratory data analysis and statistical inference. Upon completion, students can design appropriate statistical analyses, interpret results critically, and communicate findings through data-driven visualizations.
550: This course examines the historical development, core doctrines, and comparative structures of major world religions including Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Buddhism, and Hinduism. 551: This course develops students' ability to communicate complex scientific and technical concepts effectively across diverse audiences in both academic and professional contexts. 552: This course introduces students to the foundational principles of psychology within the context of cognitive science and human-computer interaction relevant to artificial intelligence development. Students examine core psychological concepts including perception, cognition, learning, memory, and decision-making processes that inform AI system design and data interpretation. The course covers empirical research methods in psychology, statistical analysis of behavioral data, and the application of psychological principles to understanding user behavior in data-driven systems. Students develop skills in experimental design, data collection, and psychological assessment techniques applicable to AI training datasets and human-centered AI evaluation. 553: This course establishes the mathematical foundations essential for advanced study in physics and artificial intelligence. 554: This course develops advanced English language proficiency tailored to scientific and technical contexts within physics and artificial intelligence. 555: This course examines the theoretical foundations and methodological approaches of cultural studies, exploring how culture functions as a system of meaning-making within societies. Students engage with key concepts including cultural production, representation, identity, and power dynamics, analyzing how cultural artifacts and practices reflect and shape social structures. The course develops critical analytical skills through close examination of texts, media, and cultural phenomena, enabling students to apply cultural theory to contemporary issues. 556: This course develops advanced Russian language proficiency for students in technical and scientific fields. Through translation exercises, composition assignments, and interactive seminars, students gain competency in articulating complex technical concepts and arguments in Russian at an intermediate-advanced level.
557: This course introduces students to core sociological concepts, theories, and research methodologies essential for understanding social structures and human behavior. Students examine classical and contemporary sociological perspectives, including functionalism, conflict theory, and symbolic interactionism, while analyzing how these frameworks apply to real-world social phenomena.
