By course completion, students can apply sociological reasoning to understand the social contexts and ethical implications of technological innovation and data-driven systems.
558: This course introduces students to core information technology concepts and their practical applications in physics and artificial intelligence research. Students learn fundamental programming principles, data structures, and algorithms while working with languages commonly used in scientific computing such as Python and C++. The course covers essential tools for data processing including version control systems, command-line interfaces, and basic database management. Through hands-on projects, students develop proficiency in writing efficient code, debugging applications, and organizing computational workflows for physics simulations and machine learning tasks. By course completion, students are equipped to apply IT fundamentals to solve computational problems in their specialized physics and AI coursework.
559: This course introduces students to fundamental economic principles and their applications in data-driven decision-making contexts relevant to physics and artificial intelligence research. Students examine microeconomic concepts including supply and demand, market structures, and resource allocation, alongside macroeconomic frameworks essential for understanding research funding, technology commercialization, and innovation ecosystems. The course develops competency in economic modeling, cost-benefit analysis, and quantitative evaluation of technological projects using statistical methods and computational tools. Students apply economic reasoning to real-world scenarios in scientific research, startup ventures, and technology development, gaining practical skills in financial planning and resource optimization for AI and physics-based initiatives.
560: This course introduces students to the formal foundations of logic essential for both physics and artificial intelligence applications. Students study propositional and predicate logic, truth tables, logical inference rules, and formal proof techniques including natural deduction and resolution methods. The course covers Boolean algebra and its applications to digital circuit design and computational systems. Through practical exercises, students develop skills in symbolic reasoning, logical argumentation, and the translation of natural language statements into formal logical expressions. Upon completion, students are able to construct rigorous logical proofs, analyze logical validity of arguments, and apply logical principles to problem-solving in physics simulations and AI reasoning systems.
561: This course introduces students to core concepts and methodologies in political science, examining political systems, institutions, governance structures, and theoretical frameworks that shape modern societies. Students analyze comparative political systems, electoral processes, policy-making mechanisms, and the relationship between state and civil society through empirical case studies and theoretical models. The course develops critical thinking skills in evaluating political phenomena and understanding how institutional design influences societal outcomes. While positioned within a data-focused program, this course provides essential domain knowledge for applying computational and AI methods to political data analysis, policy research, and governance challenges.
562: This course examines the fundamental principles governing light propagation, interaction, and manipulation in optical systems. Students explore wave optics, geometrical optics, polarization, interference, diffraction, and nonlinear optical effects, with emphasis on mathematical modeling and computational simulation. The course integrates laboratory experiments and numerical methods to analyze optical phenomena relevant to photonics and imaging technologies. Students develop proficiency in optical system design, ray tracing software, and data analysis techniques for experimental optical measurements. Upon completion, students can model complex optical systems, interpret experimental optical data, and apply optical principles to artificial intelligence applications in computer vision and photonic sensing.
563: This course covers fundamental computational methods essential for solving physics and engineering problems. Students learn numerical techniques including root-finding algorithms, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and solutions to ordinary and partial differential equations. The course emphasizes practical implementation using programming languages and scientific computing libraries, enabling students to develop efficient algorithms for complex physical simulations. By course completion, students can select appropriate numerical methods for specific problems, implement them programmatically, and analyze computational accuracy and stability. This foundation prepares students for advanced applications in physics modeling and machine learning within the program.
564: This course covers fundamental and advanced techniques in signal processing with applications to physics and artificial intelligence. Students learn time-domain and frequency-domain analysis methods, including Fourier transforms, filtering, and spectral estimation, alongside practical implementation using Python and MATLAB. The curriculum emphasizes digital signal processing fundamentals such as sampling theory, z-transforms, and discrete-time systems, with particular attention to applications in physics data analysis and machine learning pipelines. Through laboratory work and projects, students develop proficiency in designing and implementing filters, analyzing real experimental data, and integrating signal processing techniques into AI-based systems. By course completion, students can preprocess complex signals, extract meaningful features for machine learning models, and solve signal-related problems encountered in physics research and data science applications.
565: This course examines the fundamental principles of thermodynamics and statistical mechanics, bridging macroscopic observations with microscopic molecular behavior. Students study the laws of thermodynamics, entropy, free energy, phase transitions, and transport phenomena, while developing proficiency in statistical ensembles, partition functions, and probability distributions. The course emphasizes computational methods for solving thermodynamic problems and simulating physical systems using Python and numerical libraries. Students apply these concepts to real-world systems in physics and materials science, and learn how statistical physics principles underpin machine learning algorithms used in artificial intelligence applications. Upon completion, students can model complex physical systems, predict thermodynamic properties, and understand the statistical foundations connecting physics to data-driven AI methods.
566: This course explores the integration of machine learning and artificial intelligence techniques with physics-based problem solving and data analysis. Students study supervised and unsupervised learning methods, neural networks, and deep learning architectures applied to physics simulations, particle detection, and experimental data processing. The course covers practical implementation using Python libraries such as TensorFlow, PyTorch, and scikit-learn for tasks including image recognition in detector data, regression analysis for physical parameters, and optimization of complex physical systems. Students develop proficiency in preprocessing physics datasets, training predictive models, and validating results against theoretical predictions. By course completion, students can design and implement AI solutions for physics research problems, interpret model outputs in physical contexts, and critically evaluate the appropriateness of different AI methodologies for specific experimental or computational physics applications.
567: This course teaches students to develop computational models of physical phenomena using mathematical frameworks and numerical methods. Students learn to formulate differential equations governing physical systems, implement solutions using programming languages such as Python and C++, and validate results against experimental data. The course covers finite difference and finite element methods, ordinary and partial differential equations, and stability analysis of numerical schemes. Through hands-on projects, students apply modeling techniques to classical mechanics, thermodynamics, and electromagnetism problems. Upon completion, students can construct, simulate, and analyze mathematical representations of complex physical systems relevant to both physics research and machine learning applications.
568: This course provides a comprehensive introduction to quantum mechanics, covering the fundamental principles governing atomic and subatomic systems. Students study wave-particle duality, the Schrödinger equation, quantum operators, eigenvalue problems, and perturbation theory, with applications to hydrogen atoms and multi-electron systems. The course emphasizes mathematical formalism including linear algebra, complex analysis, and differential equations essential for solving quantum mechanical problems. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students develop proficiency in applying quantum mechanical principles to predict physical observables and interpret experimental results. Upon completion, students are equipped to model quantum systems relevant to materials science, quantum computing, and advanced physics applications within the data processing and AI program context.
569: Machine Learning-2 builds on foundational ML concepts to cover advanced supervised and unsupervised learning algorithms, including ensemble methods, support vector machines, neural networks, and dimensionality reduction techniques. Students implement these algorithms using Python libraries such as scikit-learn and TensorFlow, gaining practical experience in model selection, hyperparameter tuning, and cross-validation. The course emphasizes the mathematical foundations of learning theory, regularization, and optimization methods essential for understanding algorithm behavior. Students develop the ability to design end-to-end machine learning pipelines, evaluate model performance using appropriate metrics, and apply techniques to real-world datasets from physics and other domains. By course completion, students can critically assess algorithm suitability for specific problems and implement production-ready ML solutions.
570: This course covers the fundamental principles of classical mechanics, including kinematics, dynamics, and energy conservation, with applications to physical systems. Students develop proficiency in solving problems using Newton's laws, Lagrangian and Hamiltonian formalism, and rigid body dynamics. The course emphasizes mathematical techniques essential for modeling physical phenomena and provides the theoretical foundation for advanced topics in computational physics and machine learning applications to physical systems. Through problem sets and computational exercises, students learn to translate physical principles into mathematical frameworks suitable for numerical simulation and data analysis. Upon completion, students can analyze mechanical systems, derive equations of motion, and implement classical mechanics models in computational environments relevant to physics-based machine learning.
571: This course covers fundamental concepts in discrete mathematics with emphasis on graph theory and their applications in computational physics and artificial intelligence. Students study combinatorics, Boolean algebra, set theory, and formal logic, progressing to advanced graph algorithms including traversal methods, shortest path computations, and network flow analysis. The course develops proficiency in representing complex systems as graphs and applying algorithmic techniques to solve optimization problems common in machine learning and physical simulations. Through practical programming assignments, students implement classical algorithms such as Dijkstra's, Bellman-Ford, and maximum matching algorithms using Python or C++. Upon completion, students can model real-world problems as discrete structures and select appropriate algorithmic solutions for data processing tasks in physics simulations and AI applications.
572: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of probability theory and statistical methods essential for data analysis in physics and machine learning applications. Students learn probability distributions, random variables, hypothesis testing, estimation theory, and statistical inference techniques, with emphasis on applications to experimental physics and AI model evaluation. The course covers both classical frequentist and Bayesian approaches, enabling students to design experiments, analyze observational data, and quantify uncertainty in physical measurements and predictions. Through practical problem-solving, students develop competency in applying statistical tools to validate physical theories and assess machine learning model performance. By course completion, students can construct probability models, conduct rigorous statistical tests, and interpret results in the context of scientific research.
573: This course provides a rigorous foundation in single-variable calculus and real analysis, covering limits, continuity, differentiation, and integration of real functions. Students develop proficiency in computing derivatives and integrals, analyzing function behavior, and applying calculus techniques to solve physics and engineering problems. The course emphasizes both computational skills and theoretical understanding of convergence, differentiability, and the fundamental theorem of calculus. Through problem sets and applications, students build the mathematical reasoning necessary for advanced courses in physics, differential equations, and machine learning algorithms that depend on optimization and analysis of continuous functions.
574: This course covers the theory and applications of ordinary and partial differential equations essential for modeling physical systems and machine learning algorithms. Students learn analytical and numerical methods for solving first-order and higher-order differential equations, including separation of variables, integrating factors, and Fourier series techniques. The course emphasizes applications in physics such as heat diffusion, wave propagation, and quantum mechanics, as well as connections to neural network dynamics and optimization in artificial intelligence. Students develop proficiency in both symbolic computation using software tools and numerical approximation methods for solving complex differential equations. By course completion, students can formulate physical and computational problems as differential equations and apply appropriate analytical or computational techniques to obtain solutions.
575: This course develops advanced mathematical foundations essential for data processing and artificial intelligence applications in physics. Students master multivariable calculus, including partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and differential equations, alongside analytical geometry in higher dimensions. The course emphasizes computational techniques and applications to optimization problems, gradient-based methods, and geometric transformations used in machine learning algorithms. Students learn to apply these mathematical tools to solve complex physics problems and develop proficiency with symbolic computation software. Upon completion, students can formulate and solve mathematical models underlying neural networks, data transformations, and physical simulations.
576: This course covers the theory and applications of complex functions, including analytic functions, Cauchy-Riemann equations, and contour integration. Students develop proficiency in computing residues, applying the residue theorem, and evaluating real integrals through complex analysis techniques. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations and practical problem-solving methods essential for advanced physics and machine learning applications. Students learn to manipulate complex variables, understand conformal mappings, and apply these tools to solve differential equations and boundary value problems encountered in electromagnetic theory and signal processing. Upon completion, students are equipped to apply complex analysis methods to physical systems and computational algorithms in their subsequent coursework.
577: This course covers fundamental principles of electronic circuits and devices essential for data acquisition and signal processing in physics applications. Students learn semiconductor physics, transistor operation, and the design of analog circuits including amplifiers, filters, and oscillators using both discrete components and integrated circuits. The course emphasizes practical applications in sensor interfaces and data conditioning systems used in experimental physics setups. Through laboratory work, students gain hands-on experience with circuit simulation software, breadboarding, and oscilloscope measurements. Upon completion, students can design and troubleshoot basic electronic circuits, select appropriate components for signal processing tasks, and integrate electronic systems with data acquisition hardware.
578: This course introduces students to the fundamental concepts and algorithms of machine learning within the context of physics applications and data analysis. Students learn supervised learning techniques including linear regression, logistic regression, support vector machines, and decision trees, alongside unsupervised methods such as clustering and dimensionality reduction. The course covers essential mathematical foundations in linear algebra, probability, and statistics necessary for understanding model behavior and optimization. Students gain practical experience implementing algorithms using Python, scikit-learn, and Jupyter notebooks on real datasets from physics experiments and simulations. By course completion, students can preprocess data, select appropriate algorithms for specific problems, train and evaluate models, and interpret results in the context of physical phenomena.
579: This course covers the fundamental principles of electrostatics, magnetostatics, and electromagnetic induction essential for understanding physical phenomena and their computational modeling. Students study Coulomb's law, electric fields and potentials, Gauss's law, magnetic fields, Ampère's law, Faraday's induction, and Maxwell's equations, developing both analytical and numerical problem-solving skills. The course integrates computational methods for solving electromagnetic boundary value problems and simulating field distributions using numerical techniques relevant to physics-based machine learning applications. Through laboratory work and programming assignments, students learn to model electromagnetic systems, visualize field configurations, and apply these concepts to sensor design and physical data acquisition systems used in artificial intelligence pipelines. Upon completion, students can analyze complex electromagnetic systems theoretically and implement computational solutions for real-world physics problems.
580: This course introduces students to core programming concepts and procedural programming paradigms using Python as the primary language. Students learn fundamental constructs including variables, data types, control flow, functions, and basic data structures (lists, dictionaries, tuples) while developing problem-solving skills essential for scientific computing. The course emphasizes writing clean, readable code through proper naming conventions, documentation, and debugging techniques. By the end of the course, students are able to write modular programs to solve computational problems, manipulate data structures efficiently, and apply algorithmic thinking to physics and data processing applications.
581: This course extends foundational calculus concepts to multivariable functions and infinite series, essential for modeling complex physical systems and machine learning algorithms. Students study partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and convergence of series, developing the mathematical framework necessary for optimization problems in artificial intelligence and computational physics. Through rigorous proofs and problem-solving, students master techniques for analyzing functions of several variables, computing line and surface integrals, and applying theorems such as Green's, Stokes', and the divergence theorem. The course emphasizes applications to physics simulations and gradient-based optimization methods used in neural networks and data processing pipelines. By completion, students can formulate and solve differential equations arising in physical modeling and implement calculus-based algorithms in data science applications.
582: This course builds on foundational programming concepts to develop intermediate software engineering skills essential for data processing applications. Students learn object-oriented programming principles, data structures (arrays, linked lists, trees, graphs), and algorithms for sorting and searching, with emphasis on computational efficiency and complexity analysis. The course covers practical implementation using Python or C++, including file I/O operations, memory management, and debugging techniques. Through hands-on projects, students apply these concepts to solve physics-related computational problems and prepare for advanced machine learning and data analysis tasks. By course completion, students can design efficient algorithms, implement complex data structures, and write maintainable code for scientific computing applications.
583: This course covers the foundational principles of classical mechanics essential for understanding physical systems and their mathematical modeling. Students study kinematics, dynamics, conservation laws, and rotational motion, developing proficiency in vector analysis and differential equations as applied to mechanical problems. The course emphasizes both theoretical frameworks and computational approaches, including numerical simulations of mechanical systems using programming tools. Students learn to analyze real-world physical phenomena through mathematical formulation and solve complex mechanics problems relevant to data processing applications in physics. By course completion, students can model mechanical systems, apply conservation principles to physical problems, and implement computational solutions for mechanics-based simulations.
584: This course introduces students to the fundamental principles of quantum computing and quantum information theory within the context of physics-based applications. Students learn quantum mechanical foundations including superposition, entanglement, and quantum gates, and study how these principles enable quantum algorithms to solve computational problems exponentially faster than classical approaches. The course covers quantum circuit design, quantum error correction, and implementations on current quantum hardware platforms such as IBM Qiskit and other quantum simulators. Students develop practical skills in programming quantum algorithms, analyzing quantum complexity, and applying quantum computing techniques to physics simulations and optimization problems. By course completion, students can design and implement quantum algorithms, evaluate their computational advantages, and apply quantum informatics methods to real-world data processing challenges in physics and artificial intelligence.
585: This course examines the design and analysis of telecommunication systems using computational modeling techniques. Students develop proficiency in signal processing, network simulation tools, and mathematical frameworks for analyzing communication channels, modulation schemes, and system performance metrics. The course covers both classical telecommunication theory and modern digital communication protocols, with emphasis on practical implementation using MATLAB, Python, or specialized simulation software. Through laboratory work and projects, students build models of real-world telecommunication systems, including noise analysis, channel coding, and quality-of-service optimization. Upon completion, students can design telecommunication system architectures, predict system behavior under various conditions, and apply optimization techniques to improve communication efficiency.
586: This course covers the fundamental principles and practical applications of microwave electromagnetic theory in physics and engineering contexts. Students study Maxwell's equations in the microwave regime, waveguide theory, transmission line analysis, and the behavior of electromagnetic waves in bounded and unbounded media. The course emphasizes computational methods for solving microwave problems, including numerical simulations using electromagnetic modeling software and analytical techniques for cavity resonators and antenna systems. Students develop skills in designing and analyzing microwave circuits, filters, and components relevant to modern communication systems and sensor applications. By course completion, students can model microwave propagation phenomena, predict electromagnetic field distributions, and apply microwave principles to practical physics and AI-related sensing technologies.
587: This practicum course equips students with hands-on experience in designing and implementing automated experimental systems for physics research. Students learn to program microcontrollers and single-board computers (Arduino, Raspberry Pi) using C++ and Python, interface with laboratory instruments via serial communication and standard protocols (GPIB, USB), and develop data acquisition software. The course covers sensor integration, real-time signal processing, and feedback control systems essential for modern experimental physics. By course completion, students can design complete automated measurement systems, troubleshoot hardware-software integration issues, and implement automated data collection pipelines for physics experiments.
588: This course covers computational methods for modeling physical phenomena at micro and nanoscales, with emphasis on molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo simulations, and finite element analysis. Students learn to implement simulation algorithms using Python and specialized packages such as LAMMPS, GROMACS, and COMSOL, while developing proficiency in numerical methods for solving differential equations governing particle interactions and continuum mechanics. The course addresses practical applications including protein folding, crystal growth, quantum dot behavior, and thermal transport in nanostructures. Students will be able to design and execute simulations of complex systems, validate results against experimental data, and optimize computational performance for large-scale problems. By course completion, students can independently conduct research-level simulations and interpret results within the context of materials science and nanotechnology applications.
589: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical principles underlying digital signal processing and discrete systems in physics applications. Students study sampling theory, Fourier analysis of discrete signals, Z-transforms, and filter design techniques essential for processing experimental physics data. The course covers both analog-to-digital conversion fundamentals and digital filtering methods, with emphasis on applications in particle detection, spectroscopy, and sensor data analysis. Through theoretical lectures and computational exercises, students develop proficiency in implementing digital signal processing algorithms using Python or MATLAB and analyzing real physics datasets. Upon completion, students can design and implement digital processing pipelines for experimental physics measurements and understand the mathematical constraints governing signal acquisition and reconstruction.
590: This course teaches students to develop computational models for complex radiophysical phenomena using numerical methods and simulation techniques. Students learn to formulate physical problems mathematically, implement solutions using programming languages such as Python and C++, and validate results against theoretical predictions and experimental data. The course covers finite difference and finite element methods, electromagnetic field simulations, and wave propagation modeling in various media. Through practical projects, students gain proficiency in scientific computing libraries, visualization tools, and high-performance computing approaches for solving radiation and antenna problems. Upon completion, students can design, implement, and analyze computer simulations of radiophysical systems relevant to telecommunications, remote sensing, and plasma physics applications.
591: This course covers the fundamental theory and practical applications of digital signal processing (DSP) in physics and artificial intelligence contexts. Students learn discrete-time signal analysis, Fourier transforms, filter design, and spectral estimation techniques essential for processing experimental physics data and sensor inputs. The course emphasizes hands-on implementation using Python and MATLAB, where students develop algorithms for signal filtering, noise reduction, and feature extraction. Students apply DSP methods to real-world datasets from physics experiments and machine learning pipelines, gaining competency in preprocessing signals for downstream AI models. Upon completion, students can design and implement digital filters, perform frequency-domain analysis, and optimize signal quality for physics measurements and intelligent systems.
592: This course provides students with comprehensive training in the theory and implementation of neural networks for physics applications and artificial intelligence. Students learn fundamental concepts including network architectures, activation functions, backpropagation algorithms, and optimization techniques, with emphasis on applications to complex physical systems and data analysis. The course covers practical implementation using modern frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch, enabling students to design, train, and evaluate neural networks on real datasets. Students develop proficiency in convolutional neural networks, recurrent architectures, and deep learning methodologies while applying these techniques to physics-based problems such as particle detection, material property prediction, and signal processing. By course completion, students are capable of building and deploying neural network models to solve supervised and unsupervised learning problems relevant to both physics research and artificial intelligence applications.
593: This course covers fundamental and advanced optimization techniques essential for solving complex problems in physics and machine learning. Students study linear and nonlinear programming, gradient-based methods, convex optimization, and stochastic optimization algorithms including gradient descent variants and evolutionary strategies. The course emphasizes both theoretical foundations—convergence analysis, duality theory, and complexity bounds—and practical implementation using Python and specialized libraries such as SciPy and TensorFlow. Students apply optimization methods to real-world problems in physics simulations, neural network training, and parameter estimation, developing proficiency in algorithm selection, hyperparameter tuning, and performance evaluation. By course completion, students can formulate optimization problems mathematically, implement efficient solvers, and diagnose convergence issues in data-driven applications.
594: This course covers the fundamental principles of semiconductor devices and their applications in modern electronic circuits. Students learn object-oriented programming principles, data structures (arrays, linked lists, trees, graphs), and algorithms for sorting, searching, and graph traversal, with emphasis on computational complexity analysis. The course covers practical implementation of these concepts through hands-on coding projects and problem-solving exercises. Students gain proficiency in debugging, code optimization, and writing maintainable software that applies to radiophysics simulations and computational applications. By course completion, students can design and implement efficient algorithms, analyze algorithmic performance, and develop robust applications for scientific computing tasks.
655: This course extends foundational calculus concepts to multivariable functions and infinite series. Students study partial derivatives, multiple integrals, vector calculus, and convergence of series and sequences in rigorous mathematical frameworks. The course develops proficiency in computing limits, derivatives, and integrals for complex functions while applying these tools to optimization problems and physical applications. Upon completion, students can analyze multivariable systems, solve differential equations, and apply mathematical analysis techniques to problems in radiophysics and signal processing.
656: This course equips radiophysics and computer technology students with systematic approaches to designing and conducting scientific research. Students learn fundamental research methodologies, including hypothesis formulation, experimental design, data collection protocols, and statistical analysis techniques applicable to electromagnetic phenomena and computational systems. The course covers research planning tools such as literature review strategies, project management frameworks, and documentation standards essential for academic and industrial research environments. Students develop practical skills in designing experiments, selecting appropriate measurement instruments, analyzing results using computational methods, and presenting findings in peer-reviewed formats. Upon completion, students are prepared to independently plan and execute research projects in radiophysics, signal processing, and related technological domains.
657: This course covers the foundational principles of classical mechanics essential for radiophysics and computer technology applications. Students study kinematics, dynamics, energy conservation, momentum, rotational motion, and oscillatory systems through both theoretical frameworks and mathematical formalism. The course emphasizes vector analysis, differential equations, and problem-solving techniques applied to mechanical systems relevant to electromagnetic wave propagation and signal processing. Students develop competency in analyzing mechanical phenomena using calculus-based methods and applying these concepts to understand physical systems underlying modern communication technologies. Laboratory work reinforces theoretical concepts through experimental measurement and data analysis.
658: This course introduces students to core programming concepts and procedural programming paradigms using C/C++ as the primary language. Students learn fundamental constructs including variables, data types, control flow structures, functions, arrays, and pointers, while developing problem-solving skills through algorithmic thinking. The course emphasizes hands-on coding practice with compiler tools and debugging techniques to write, test, and optimize basic programs. By course completion, students can design and implement procedural solutions to computational problems and understand memory management principles essential for systems-level programming in radiophysics applications.
659: This course covers the design and implementation of digital systems using programmable logic devices and microcontrollers. Students learn hardware description languages (HDL) such as VHDL or Verilog to model and simulate digital circuits, alongside practical programming of field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) and embedded systems. The course emphasizes the integration of hardware and software components, including interrupt handling, real-time processing, and interfacing with external peripherals. Students develop proficiency in development tools, debugging techniques, and optimization strategies for resource-constrained environments. By course completion, students can design, prototype, and deploy programmable electronic systems for signal processing and control applications relevant to radiophysics applications.
660: Students engage in supervised practical training at research institutes, technology companies, or university laboratories aligned with radiophysics and computer technology specializations. The course develops hands-on competency in experimental design, measurement instrumentation, data acquisition systems, and signal processing techniques relevant to electromagnetic phenomena and computational applications. Participants apply theoretical knowledge to real-world problems in antenna design, microwave engineering, wireless communications, or computational modeling while documenting technical findings and presenting results. Upon completion, students demonstrate proficiency in laboratory protocols, technical report writing, and collaborative problem-solving within professional research and development environments.
661: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of artificial intelligence principles, architectures, and applications within the context of radiophysics and computational systems. Students learn fundamental AI concepts including machine learning algorithms, neural networks, natural language processing, and computer vision, with emphasis on their implementation in signal processing and electromagnetic systems. The course covers practical programming in Python and relevant AI frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch) for developing intelligent systems that analyze and interpret complex physical data. Students develop skills in designing and training AI models for pattern recognition, classification, and prediction tasks relevant to radiophysics applications. By course completion, students are capable of implementing AI solutions for real-world problems in signal detection, data analysis, and autonomous system control.
662: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of digital logic design and microprocessor architecture. Students learn Boolean algebra, logic gates, combinational and sequential circuits, and design methodologies using hardware description languages (HDL). The course covers microprocessor organization, instruction sets, assembly language programming, and memory hierarchies, with practical implementation on FPGA platforms and microcontroller boards. Through laboratory exercises and design projects, students develop proficiency in circuit simulation tools, debugging techniques, and low-level system programming. Upon completion, students can design digital circuits, write assembly code, and understand the fundamental principles underlying modern computing systems.
663: This course examines the architecture, protocols, and applications of Internet of Things (IoT) systems within embedded and networked environments. Students study wireless communication standards (WiFi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, LoRaWAN), sensor integration, microcontroller programming, and cloud connectivity frameworks essential for IoT deployment. The course covers IoT platform design, data acquisition and processing, security considerations, and real-time system constraints through both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. Students develop functional IoT applications using industry-standard development boards and platforms, gaining hands-on experience with hardware-software integration and network communication. Upon completion, students can design, prototype, and deploy IoT solutions for real-world applications in smart systems, environmental monitoring, and industrial automation.
664: This course examines the fundamental principles and architecture of modern mobile communication networks, including cellular systems, wireless protocols, and network infrastructure. Students study signal propagation, modulation techniques, multiple access schemes (CDMA, TDMA, OFDMA), and the evolution from 2G through 5G technologies. The course covers practical aspects of mobile system design, including channel modeling, interference management, and quality of service optimization. Through laboratory work and simulations, students develop proficiency in analyzing mobile network performance, designing communication links, and using industry-standard tools for system evaluation. Upon completion, students are able to evaluate mobile communication systems, troubleshoot network issues, and apply theoretical knowledge to emerging wireless technologies.
665: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical methodologies for simulating complex telecommunication systems. Students develop proficiency in mathematical modeling techniques, signal processing algorithms, and network simulation tools to analyze system performance under various operating conditions. The course covers modulation schemes, channel modeling, noise analysis, and interference effects using software platforms such as MATLAB and specialized telecommunication simulators. Through hands-on projects, students design and evaluate telecommunication architectures, predict system behavior, and optimize parameters for improved reliability and efficiency. Upon completion, students can construct realistic models of communication systems, interpret simulation results, and apply findings to solve real-world telecommunication engineering problems.
666: This course examines the fundamental principles and practical applications of electromagnetic wave propagation in the microwave frequency range. Students study waveguide theory, transmission line analysis, impedance matching techniques, and the design of microwave components including filters, couplers, and antennas. The course covers both theoretical electromagnetic field equations and computational methods for solving microwave problems using simulation software. Through laboratory work and design projects, students develop proficiency in measuring microwave parameters, analyzing S-parameters, and prototyping microwave circuits and systems. Upon completion, students are capable of designing and optimizing microwave devices for communication systems, radar applications, and wireless technologies.
667: This course covers computational modeling and simulation techniques for physical and chemical processes occurring at micro and nanoscales. Students learn to apply molecular dynamics, Monte Carlo methods, and finite element analysis to predict behavior of nanostructures, quantum systems, and biomolecules. The course emphasizes practical implementation using MATLAB, COMSOL, and specialized simulation software such as LAMMPS and GROMACS. Students develop proficiency in designing simulation experiments, validating computational results against experimental data, and interpreting output to extract material properties and system dynamics. By course completion, students can construct and execute multi-scale simulations relevant to nanotechnology, materials science, and semiconductor device engineering.
668: This course provides hands-on training in designing and implementing automated experimental systems using modern control hardware and software. Students learn to interface sensors and actuators with computers, program data acquisition systems, and develop real-time monitoring applications using languages such as Python, C++, and LabVIEW. Through practical laboratory exercises, students gain proficiency in signal processing, feedback control loops, and troubleshooting automated measurement setups. Upon completion, students are able to design complete automation solutions for physics and engineering experiments, integrate multiple instruments into unified systems, and analyze experimental data with automated workflows.
669: This course examines the principles and design of modern digital communication systems, covering modulation techniques, channel coding, and signal detection methods. Students study fundamental concepts including pulse amplitude modulation (PAM), quadrature amplitude modulation (QAM), frequency shift keying (FSK), and phase shift keying (PSK), alongside error-correcting codes such as Hamming codes and convolutional codes. The course develops practical skills in analyzing communication system performance metrics including bit error rate (BER), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and bandwidth efficiency through both theoretical analysis and computational simulations using MATLAB or Python. Students design and implement digital receivers, equalization techniques, and synchronization algorithms to recover transmitted information from noisy channels. Upon completion, students can evaluate trade-offs between spectral efficiency and power efficiency, and apply these concepts to contemporary wireless and wired communication systems.
670: This course examines the fundamental physics and engineering principles of semiconductor devices and their application in nanosensor technology. Students study band theory, carrier transport mechanisms, and the design of p-n junctions, field-effect transistors, and photodetectors, with emphasis on nanoscale device behavior and quantum effects. The course covers fabrication techniques including lithography, etching, and deposition methods used in semiconductor manufacturing and nanodevice production. Students develop practical skills in device characterization, simulation using SPICE and TCAD software, and analysis of sensor performance metrics such as sensitivity, noise, and response time. Upon completion, students can design and evaluate semiconductor-based nanosensors for applications in environmental monitoring, biomedical diagnostics, and physical parameter detection.
671: This course examines the principles and applications of optoelectronic devices and their integration into renewable energy systems. Students study semiconductor physics, photovoltaic cells, light-emitting diodes, photodetectors, and laser systems, alongside solar energy conversion technologies and energy storage mechanisms. The course covers practical design and analysis of optoelectronic circuits, photovoltaic system modeling, and efficiency optimization techniques using computational tools. Students develop competency in selecting appropriate optoelectronic components for renewable energy applications and evaluating system performance through both theoretical calculations and laboratory measurements. By course completion, students can design and analyze integrated optoelectronic-renewable energy systems and understand the fundamental physics governing light-matter interactions in energy conversion devices.
672: This course examines fundamental and applied techniques for synthesizing crystalline materials across multiple scales, from bulk crystals to nanometer-scale structures. Students study growth mechanisms including Czochralski and Bridgman methods for volumetric crystals, physical and chemical vapor deposition for thin films, and sol-gel, molecular beam epitaxy, and hydrothermal synthesis for nanostructures. The course covers process parameters, thermodynamic principles, and characterization methods such as X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and atomic force microscopy. Students gain practical experience with growth equipment operation, process optimization, and quality assessment of synthesized materials. Upon completion, students can design and execute crystal growth experiments, troubleshoot synthesis problems, and select appropriate techniques for specific material and application requirements.
673: This course examines the fundamental physics, engineering principles, and manufacturing technologies underlying composite materials used in modern applications. Students study the structure-property relationships of fiber-reinforced polymers, ceramic matrix composites, and metal matrix composites, including stress transfer mechanisms, failure modes, and anisotropic behavior. The course covers fabrication techniques such as hand layup, resin transfer molding, filament winding, and automated fiber placement, alongside characterization methods including mechanical testing, microscopy, and non-destructive evaluation. Students develop competency in composite design calculations, laminate theory, and failure prediction using analytical and computational approaches. Upon completion, students can select appropriate composite materials for engineering applications, design composite structures, and troubleshoot manufacturing and performance issues in composite systems.
674: This course covers the fundamental principles of microelectronic device physics, semiconductor materials, and integrated circuit fabrication processes. Students learn the design and simulation of digital and analog circuits using industry-standard tools such as SPICE and hardware description languages (HDL), with emphasis on CMOS technology and logic gate implementation. The course addresses practical aspects of chip layout, design rules, power consumption optimization, and signal integrity in modern nanoscale devices. Through hands-on projects, students design functional circuits from specification to layout and gain proficiency in electronic design automation (EDA) software. Upon completion, students are able to analyze semiconductor device behavior, design optimized integrated circuits, and understand the trade-offs between performance, power, and area in chip design.
675: This course covers the fundamental principles and methodologies for modeling integrated circuits at various levels of abstraction. Students learn semiconductor physics fundamentals, device modeling (MOSFET, BJT, diodes), and circuit simulation techniques using industry-standard tools such as SPICE and Verilog-A. The course emphasizes both behavioral and physical modeling approaches, enabling students to develop accurate models for analog, digital, and mixed-signal circuits. Through practical assignments, students gain proficiency in parameter extraction, model validation, and optimization for circuit design applications. Upon completion, students are able to create, validate, and implement IC models for use in circuit simulation and design verification workflows.
676: This course covers the theoretical foundations and practical aspects of wireless communication systems, including signal propagation, modulation techniques, and channel characteristics. Students examine electromagnetic wave behavior in free space and complex environments, analyzing path loss, fading, and interference phenomena that affect wireless transmission. The course introduces modulation schemes such as AM, FM, and digital modulations (PSK, QAM), along with fundamental concepts of coding and error correction. Through laboratory work and simulations, students develop proficiency in designing and analyzing wireless communication links, calculating link budgets, and evaluating system performance metrics. Upon completion, students can model wireless channels, select appropriate modulation and coding schemes for specific applications, and predict communication system reliability under various propagation conditions.
677: This course examines the principles of computer network architecture, protocols, and communication systems, with emphasis on the OSI and TCP/IP models. Students study network security threats, cryptographic techniques, authentication mechanisms, and firewall technologies to protect data integrity and confidentiality. The course covers practical implementation of network protocols, packet analysis using tools such as Wireshark, and configuration of secure network infrastructure. Students develop skills in vulnerability assessment, intrusion detection, and secure system administration while analyzing real-world cybersecurity incidents. Upon completion, students are able to design secure networks, implement encryption protocols, and diagnose network security vulnerabilities in modern computing environments.
678: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of radio and television transmission systems, covering electromagnetic wave propagation, modulation techniques (AM, FM, digital), and signal processing principles. Students learn the architecture and operation of broadcast transmitters and receivers, antenna design fundamentals, and frequency allocation standards. Through laboratory work, students gain practical experience with RF measurement equipment, oscilloscopes, and spectrum analyzers to analyze and troubleshoot radio and television circuits. The course emphasizes the transition from analog to digital broadcasting standards, including DVB-T and modern compression techniques. Upon completion, students can design basic RF circuits, interpret broadcast specifications, and understand the technical infrastructure underlying contemporary radio and television systems.
679: This practicum course provides hands-on experience in designing, implementing, and testing telecommunications systems and networks. Students work with industry-standard tools and equipment to develop practical skills in signal transmission, modulation techniques, network protocols, and data communication systems. Through laboratory exercises and projects, students gain proficiency in configuring telecommunications hardware, analyzing signal characteristics using oscilloscopes and spectrum analyzers, and troubleshooting network connectivity issues. The course emphasizes the integration of theoretical knowledge from radiophysics with practical telecommunications engineering, preparing students to work on real-world communication infrastructure and systems. By course completion, students can design basic communication circuits, optimize transmission parameters, and implement solutions for common telecommunications challenges.
680: This course examines the mathematical foundations and practical principles underlying digital signal processing and computation. Students study discrete-time signals, sampling theory, z-transforms, and digital filter design, gaining proficiency in analyzing and implementing algorithms for signal manipulation. The course covers Fourier analysis in the digital domain, including the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT), and explores applications in communications, audio processing, and data acquisition systems. Through theoretical analysis and computational exercises, students develop the ability to design, simulate, and optimize digital systems for real-world radiophysics and telecommunications applications.
681: This course develops students' ability to solve complex radiophysical problems through computational simulation and numerical methods. Students learn to model electromagnetic wave propagation, antenna systems, and signal processing phenomena using specialized software tools and programming languages such as MATLAB and Python. The course covers finite difference time domain (FDTD) methods, method of moments, and other numerical techniques essential for analyzing radiophysical systems. Students apply these computational approaches to design and optimize antennas, analyze wave interactions with materials, and simulate real-world radiophysical scenarios. By course completion, students can independently formulate radiophysical problems mathematically, implement efficient numerical solutions, and validate results through computational experiments.
682: This course examines the design, analysis, and operation of radio technical systems used in communication, radar, and navigation applications. Students study electromagnetic wave propagation, antenna theory, signal modulation and demodulation techniques, and receiver/transmitter architectures. The course covers practical implementation using software tools for circuit simulation and signal processing, including MATLAB and specialized RF design software. Students develop competency in calculating system performance parameters, designing filter networks, and troubleshooting real-world radio systems. By course completion, students can design functional radio technical systems, analyze system specifications, and apply electromagnetic principles to solve engineering problems in wireless communications and detection systems.
683: This course examines the principles and applications of microelectronic devices and circuits within the context of millimeter-wave and terahertz (GBH) technologies. Students study semiconductor physics, transistor design, and integrated circuit fabrication techniques specific to high-frequency applications, including field-effect transistors (FETs), heterojunction bipolar transistors (HBTs), and monolithic microwave integrated circuits (MMICs). The course covers circuit design methodologies for low-noise amplifiers, oscillators, and mixers operating in the GHz-THz frequency range. Students develop practical skills in computer-aided design (CAD) tools for circuit simulation and layout, and gain hands-on experience with characterization and testing of high-frequency microelectronic components. Upon completion, students are able to design, analyze, and optimize microelectronic circuits for advanced communication and sensing systems.
684: This course covers the fundamental theory and practical applications of digital signal processing (DSP) in radiophysics and communication systems. Students learn discrete-time signal analysis, z-transforms, discrete Fourier transforms (DFT), and filter design techniques including FIR and IIR filter implementation. The course emphasizes hands-on experience with DSP algorithms using MATLAB and C/C++, enabling students to develop real-time signal processing applications for radar, communications, and sensor systems. Upon completion, students can design and implement digital filters, perform spectral analysis, and optimize signal processing pipelines for embedded systems relevant to radiophysics applications.
685: This course examines the fundamental principles and industrial processes for manufacturing semiconductor materials and devices. Students study crystal growth techniques, doping methods, and purification processes essential for producing high-quality semiconductors, alongside the physics of p-n junctions, transistors, and integrated circuits. The course covers photolithography, etching, deposition, and metallization technologies used in device fabrication, with emphasis on how process parameters affect device performance and reliability. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students develop practical skills in characterizing semiconductor properties and analyzing manufacturing defects. Upon completion, students can design basic semiconductor devices, optimize fabrication processes, and troubleshoot common manufacturing issues in semiconductor production.
686: This course examines the fundamental physics governing semiconductor materials and devices, covering band theory, charge carrier dynamics, and the physics of p-n junctions. Students develop proficiency in analyzing semiconductor behavior through energy band diagrams, carrier transport mechanisms (drift and diffusion), and recombination processes. The course integrates theoretical principles with practical applications in diodes, transistors, and integrated circuits, utilizing computational tools for device simulation and characterization. Upon completion, students can predict semiconductor device performance, design basic circuits using semiconductor components, and apply quantum mechanical concepts to explain device operation at the microscopic level.
687: This course covers the theoretical foundations and computational methods for modeling electromagnetic phenomena across various frequency ranges and physical scales. Students learn to formulate Maxwell's equations in different coordinate systems, apply numerical techniques such as the finite difference time domain (FDTD) method and finite element method (FEM), and implement simulations using specialized software packages. The course emphasizes the analysis of wave propagation, scattering, radiation patterns, and field interactions in complex geometries relevant to antenna design, microwave devices, and electromagnetic compatibility. Through practical laboratory work, students develop proficiency in electromagnetic simulation tools and validate computational results against analytical solutions and experimental data. Upon completion, students can design and optimize electromagnetic systems, troubleshoot simulation models, and interpret results for engineering applications in radiophysics and telecommunications.
688: This course examines the theoretical foundations and practical implementation of secure communication systems within modern information networks. Students study cryptographic algorithms, including symmetric and asymmetric encryption methods, digital signatures, and authentication protocols, alongside their mathematical underpinnings in number theory and abstract algebra. The course covers key distribution mechanisms, secure channel establishment, and vulnerability analysis in communication protocols, with emphasis on real-world applications in network security. Through laboratory work, students implement cryptographic systems using industry-standard tools and programming languages, analyze potential attack vectors, and design secure communication architectures. Upon completion, students can evaluate security requirements for communication systems, select appropriate cryptographic solutions, and develop protocols resistant to common threats in radiophysics and computer technology applications.
689: This course provides students with foundational knowledge of telecommunications systems and signal transmission principles essential to radiophysics and computer technology. Students study modulation techniques, signal encoding, channel characteristics, and noise effects on communication systems, developing proficiency in analyzing and designing basic telecommunication circuits. The course covers analog and digital transmission methods, including amplitude modulation (AM), frequency modulation (FM), and digital modulation schemes, with practical applications in radio and wireless systems. Through laboratory work and problem-solving exercises, students gain hands-on experience with telecommunications equipment and software tools for signal analysis and system simulation. Upon completion, students are able to evaluate telecommunication system performance, select appropriate modulation schemes for specific applications, and apply fundamental concepts to more advanced courses in radio engineering and signal processing.
690: This course provides students with comprehensive knowledge of computer network architecture, protocols, and design principles. Students study the OSI and TCP/IP models, learning how data transmission occurs across network layers, and gain practical experience with network configuration tools such as Cisco packet tracer and network analyzers. The course covers essential protocols including IP, TCP, UDP, DNS, and HTTP, along with network security fundamentals and routing algorithms. Through hands-on laboratory work, students design and troubleshoot small-scale networks, configure switches and routers, and analyze network traffic using packet capture tools. Upon completion, students are able to implement basic network topologies, diagnose connectivity issues, and apply foundational security practices in networked systems.
691: This course examines the fundamental principles of electron emission, transport, and interaction in vacuum and semiconductor devices. Students study thermionic emission, photoelectric effect, secondary emission, and the physics of electron beams in vacuum tubes, cathode ray tubes, and microwave devices. The course covers semiconductor junction physics, band theory, carrier dynamics, and the operational principles of diodes, transistors, and integrated circuits. Through laboratory work and problem-solving, students develop skills in analyzing electron trajectories, calculating device characteristics, and designing basic electronic circuits. Upon completion, students can predict device behavior under various operating conditions and apply physical principles to select and optimize electronic components for radiophysics applications.
